l1.question: A GP refers a client with the note: "Meets 6 of the 9 DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder — diagnosis is clear." According to Lecture 1, what has the DSM classification done, and what has it not done yet?

options.text: It has provided the diagnosis; only a treatment plan is still missing.
It has explained why the problem persists, but not how severe it is.
It has described a symptom pattern, but not explained its development or persistence.
It has identified the underlying mechanism, but not the client's wider context.

l1.explanation: DSM/ICD describe criteria (symptoms, duration, severity, distress, impairment) and are used for classification. The slide says explicitly that they do not explain why the problem developed/persists in this person and do not provide a diagnosis → A is wrong (classification ≠ diagnosis). B is wrong: the DSM does describe severity, but does not explain. D is wrong: finding mechanisms is the RDoC ambition, not what the DSM does.

l1.question:
Evaluate the two statements about RDoC.
I. RDoC was developed as a new clinical classification system that replaces the DSM in daily practice.
II. RDoC encourages measuring functioning across several units of analysis, such as genes, circuits, behaviour and self-report.

options.text: Only statement II is correct.
Only statement I is correct.
Both statements are correct.
Both statements are incorrect.

l1.explanation: I is false: "RDoC does not replace classification, it adds a transdiagnostic research perspective" and it is "not a ready-to-use clinical classification system" (formal clinical classification is listed as a limitation). II is true: its "measurement strategy" is to measure across multiple levels (the 8 units of analysis) and triangulate.

l1.question: Which of the following is not one of the HiTOP spectra discussed in the lecture?

options.text: Detachment
Somatoform
Antagonistic externalizing
Negative valence

l1.explanation: Negative valence is an RDoC domain (with positive valence, cognitive systems, social processes, arousal/regulation, sensorimotor). The six HiTOP spectra are internalising, thought disorder, detachment, disinhibited externalising, antagonistic externalising and somatoform.

l1.question: In a client's personal symptom network, "worrying" turns out to have the most and strongest connections with the other symptoms. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: Worrying causes the other symptoms, so treating it will make the disorder disappear.
Worrying is a central symptom and possible target, but centrality does not prove causation.
Worrying is a bridge symptom, because it has so many connections with others.
Worrying is the latent factor that produces the other symptoms in this network.

l1.explanation: A central symptom = many or strong connections; the slide adds "this does not automatically imply causality" (limitation: central symptom ≠ cause) → A is wrong. C mixes up the definitions: a bridge symptom connects two problem clusters; "many connections" defines centrality. D uses the DSM/latent-factor logic that the network approach rejects.

l1.question: According to the problem-sustaining pattern (PSP) view of Voerman et al. (2025), professional care is warranted when…

options.text: the number of symptoms exceeds the DSM threshold for two weeks.
the behaviour deviates from what is statistically normal in the culture.
an underlying biological or psychological dysfunction has been identified in them.
the person's own problem-solving efforts have become stuck in a repeating pattern.

l1.explanation: The PSP demarcation replaces "normal | abnormal" with "productive → getting stuck": "care is warranted when the person's own problem-solving efforts become stuck". A, B and C all belong to the classical question ("Is this normal or pathological?"), which draws boundaries around symptoms and looks for underlying dysfunctions.

l1.question:
Evaluate the two statements about symptom networks.
I. A network estimated in a large group of patients shows how the symptoms are connected within each individual patient of that group.
II. In a network based on data from a single time point, you may draw arrows showing which symptom causes which, as long as the edges are thick enough.

options.text: Both statements are incorrect.
Only statement I is correct.
Only statement II is correct.
Both statements are correct.

l1.explanation: I: "Group-level network ≠ individual client network" (a listed limitation). II: thickness only shows the strength of an association; direction can only be claimed "with longitudinal data or a theoretical basis for causality". One time point = no direction, however thick the edge.

l1.question: A psychologist wonders: "Which processes — such as reward learning and working memory — function differently in this client, and can I measure them with lab tasks and physiology as well as with a questionnaire?" Which perspective is she using?

options.text: The HiTOP model
The network approach
The RDoC framework
Pattern diagnostics approach

l1.explanation: Reward learning and working memory are RDoC constructs; measuring with paradigms (tasks), physiology and self-report are RDoC units of analysis. RDoC's question: "Which processes or domains are functioning differently, and how can we measure them?" HiTOP asks about severity within spectra; network about symptoms reinforcing each other; PSP about patterns that block problem-solving.

l1.question: Client 1 with "major depressive disorder" sleeps too little, has lost weight and feels very guilty. Client 2 with the same classification sleeps 12 hours a day, has gained weight and mainly feels no pleasure anymore. Which limitation of categorical classification does this illustrate most directly?

options.text: Diagnostic comorbidity
Symptom heterogeneity
Diagnostic instability
Arbitrary boundaries

l1.explanation: Heterogeneity = two people with the same diagnosis differ strongly in symptoms (and care needs/mechanisms). Comorbidity = several disorders at once; instability = diagnoses change over time while vulnerabilities persist; arbitrary boundaries = "just below threshold" cases are hard to classify. Heterogeneity is listed as a reason for RDoC, HiTOP and the network approach.

l1.question: The lecture showed a study by Vos & Everaert (2025) linking HiTOP dimensions to interpretation biases. Which conclusion fits the results shown?

options.text: Negative interpretation bias was related to the general p-factor rather than the internalizing spectrum.
Negative interpretation bias was related only to the internalizing spectrum, as expected for anxiety.
Detachment was related to a stronger positive interpretation bias in the results shown.
None of the interpretation biases was significantly related to any of the HiTOP dimensions.

l1.explanation: The p-factor predicted negative interpretation bias (0.28, p < .001) and negative interpretation inflexibility (0.28, p < .001); internalizing was not significant (0.36, p = .353) → B wrong. Detachment was related to less positive interpretation bias (−0.23, p = .030) → C wrong, and D is wrong because there were significant effects. Take-away: the bias looks transdiagnostic.

l1.question: Which statement about the RDoC framework is not correct?

options.text: The rows are functional domains, such as negative valence and cognitive systems.
Constructs are specific functions within a domain, such as acute threat.
The matrix is embedded within development and the wider environment, not isolated.
The matrix is fixed: domains were defined once and are not revised.

l1.explanation: The slide: "RDoC is dynamic: the matrix is updated as scientific research evolves." A, B and C are all correct descriptions (rows = domains; constructs = specific functions within a domain; don't forget development and environment/context).

l1.question: Voerman et al. (2025) want to keep the valuable functions of the concept "mental disorder" but reduce its design flaws. Which option lists only design flaws?

options.text: Stigma · recognition of suffering and effort · reification of categories
Individualising social problems · reification · power dynamics and iatrogenic effects
Weak external validity of syndromes · evidence-informed treatment recommendations · stigma
Access to specialised care · pathologisation of diversity · power dynamics

l1.explanation: Design flaws: stigma and pathologisation of diversity; individualising complex social problems; reification; weak external validity of syndromes; power dynamics and iatrogenic effects. Functions to preserve: recognition of suffering and effort (A), evidence-informed treatment recommendations (C), access to specialised care (D), an understandable explanation, measuring outcomes. Each of A, C and D sneaks in one function.

l1.question: A trainee ticks off DSM criteria during an intake — "five of nine, so depression" — without asking what these symptoms mean for the client or when and in which situations they occur. Which pitfall–alternative pair from the slide "Psychological assessment is not…" fits best?

options.text: Classifying too soon → carefully communicating findings to the client
Reducing the client to a label → testing hypotheses carefully
"Counting" symptoms without any meaning → understanding patterns and context
Ignoring contextual information → clarifying the client's request for help

l1.explanation: The slide pairs are: classifying too soon ↔ clarifying the request for help; ignoring context ↔ testing hypotheses; counting symptoms without meaning ↔ understanding patterns and context; reducing the client to a label ↔ carefully communicating findings. Options A, B and D mismatch the pairs. The trainee is literally counting symptoms without asking about meaning/situations → C.

l1.question: Sara (29, teacher) has felt low for four months. She sleeps badly, worries about work and avoids friends since a conflict with her principal. Which question follows most directly from the HiTOP lens?

options.text: Which of her symptoms keep each other going in feedback loops?
How high does she score on internalising, perhaps with some detachment?
Which processes of reward and threat work differently in her?
Does she meet enough DSM criteria for at least two weeks?

l1.explanation: HiTOP gives a severity profile on dimensions (here probably high internalising, maybe some detachment) instead of a yes/no. A is the network lens, C is RDoC, and D is the DSM/ICD lens.

l1.question: Sara (29, teacher) has felt low for four months. She sleeps badly, worries about work and avoids friends since a conflict with her principal. Which question follows most directly from the network lens?

options.text: Which processes of reward and threat work differently in her now?
How high does she score on internalising, perhaps with some detachment?
What has she tried so far, and when did that help?
Is poor sleep a bridge between her worry and low mood?

l1.explanation: The network lens asks which symptoms keep each other going (worry, poor sleep, fatigue, withdrawal, low mood) and where to intervene, for example at a bridge such as sleep. A is RDoC, B is HiTOP, and C is pattern diagnostics.

l1.question: Sara (29, teacher) has felt low for four months. She sleeps badly, worries about work and avoids friends since a conflict with her principal. Which question follows most directly from pattern diagnostics (PSP)?

options.text: What has she tried so far, and when did that help?
Does she meet enough DSM criteria for at least two weeks?
Is poor sleep a bridge between her worry and low mood?
How high does she score on internalising, perhaps with some detachment?

l1.explanation: Pattern diagnostics asks what no longer works, what is at stake, what she has already tried and when it helped, and which interactions keep the problem going. B is DSM/ICD, C is the network lens, and D is HiTOP.

l1.question: A father says: "The school psychologist diagnosed our son with ADHD, so now we finally know what's going on." According to Lecture 1, what does the label do and not do?

options.text: It names a pattern and explains its cause, but gives no support.
It opens doors to support and explains why now, but names nothing.
It names a symptom pattern and opens doors, but not why now.
It describes strengths and context and opens doors, but names nothing.

l1.explanation: ADHD is a classification: a symptom pattern that meets agreed criteria. It works like a key (acknowledgement, support, shared language), but it does not explain why this boy has problems now, and it says nothing about his strengths or context. A wrongly says it explains the cause, B denies its practical use, and D reverses what a label does.

l1.question: The school psychologist has just diagnosed a boy with ADHD, and his father feels relieved. According to Lecture 1, what should happen next?

options.text: Ask what the label means for this child, in this context, now.
Check that the criteria were applied correctly, then plan the treatment.
Place his symptoms on dimensions to estimate how severe they are.
Map which symptoms keep each other going, then pick one to target.

l1.explanation: Classification is a tool, not an endpoint. The core clinical question is what this means for this child, in this context, at this time, so the assessment continues (explanations such as sleep, stress or classroom, strengths, needed help). B skips that question and goes straight to treatment, C is the HiTOP lens and D the network lens; both are possible later tools but not the next step.

l1.question: Tom (21) has a thesis deadline. Since his breakup he postpones work, games until 4 a.m., sleeps until noon, feels "a failure" and skips meetings with his supervisor. He made strict daily schedules twice, but gave up after two days. In a pattern-diagnostic (PSP) analysis, in which step do the failed strict schedules belong?

options.text: Step one: the problem and what is at stake
Step three: the repeating and self-reinforcing pattern behind it
Step four: the feasible entry point for an intervention
Step two: the attempts already made to solve it

l1.explanation: The strict schedules (which failed, probably because the step was too big) are his own attempts at a solution. The problem step describes what no longer works and what is at stake, the pattern step describes the loop that keeps it going, and the entry point is where an intervention could start.

l1.question: Tom (21) has a thesis deadline. Since his breakup he postpones work, games until 4 a.m., sleeps until noon, feels "a failure" and skips meetings with his supervisor. He made strict daily schedules twice, but gave up after two days. Which description is the best pattern in the PSP sense?

options.text: Breakup causes low mood, which causes avoidance, which causes the missed meetings.
Low discipline explains his gaming, his late sleeping and his skipped meetings.
Stress leads to avoidance, relief, fewer successes, shame, poor sleep, more avoidance.
A depressive disorder explains his withdrawal, his poor sleep and low mood.

l1.explanation: A PSP pattern is a repeating, self-reinforcing loop that crosses bio, psycho and social areas: stress, avoidance, short relief, fewer successes, shame, disturbed sleep, less energy, more avoidance. A is a one-way chain, B is a trait explanation, and D is a classification, not a loop.

l1.question: Tom (21) has a thesis deadline. Since his breakup he postpones work, games until 4 a.m., sleeps until noon, feels "a failure" and skips meetings with his supervisor. He made strict daily schedules twice, but gave up after two days. Which entry point for an evidence-informed intervention is most feasible?

options.text: Agree a fixed two-week schedule with set hours for work and sleep.
First restore his sleep rhythm and then add small activating steps.
Start by challenging his belief that he is a complete failure.
Focus first on processing the breakup before turning to his work.

l1.explanation: The entry point is where the loop can be broken most feasibly, for example restoring the sleep rhythm, small activating steps, one short meeting with the supervisor, or telling one friend. A repeats the earlier failed attempt (too big a step), C targets a thought instead of the first feasible step, and D postpones the work part of the loop.

l1.question: A researcher estimates a network of depression and anxiety symptoms in 800 patients at one time point. "Irritability" is the only node linking the anxiety items to the depression items. How should it be described?

options.text: A central symptom, which is relevant for explaining overall severity
A latent factor, which is relevant for explaining shared variance
A feedback loop, which is relevant for explaining symptom persistence
A bridge symptom, which is relevant for explaining comorbidity

l1.explanation: A node that connects two clusters of symptoms is a bridge symptom, which is relevant for comorbidity. Central means many or strong connections overall, a latent factor is not a node in a network, and a feedback loop is a set of symptoms that reciprocally maintain each other.

l1.question: A researcher estimates a network of depression and anxiety symptoms in 800 patients at one time point. "Rumination", "sleep problems" and "fatigue" are all strongly connected to each other. What does this show?

options.text: A feedback loop, where the symptoms may maintain one another
A bridge, where the symptoms may connect two separate clusters
A central node, where the symptoms may all depend on one
A latent disorder, where the symptoms may all reflect it

l1.explanation: Strong reciprocal connections among a few symptoms suggest a feedback loop, where each symptom may keep the others going. A bridge links two different clusters, a central symptom is defined by its many connections, and a latent disorder is the common-cause idea that the network approach questions.

l1.question: A researcher estimates a network of depression and anxiety symptoms in 800 patients at one time point. Which statement about what a clinician may conclude from this network is correct?

options.text: It indicates individual dynamics, because the sample was very large and diverse.
It is a hypothesis, because item choice and measurement error shape it.
It identifies causal drivers, because central symptoms are always the treatment targets.
It shows the temporal order, because the edges have a direction here.

l1.explanation: A group network estimated at one time point is a hypothesis. The chosen items and measurement error shape the result, and it never replaces risk assessment or classification. A confuses a group network with an individual network, C treats central symptoms as proven causes, and D forgets that one time point gives no temporal order or direction.

l1.question: Lisa says after receiving her classification: "Finally a name! So I'm not lazy or crazy." Which function of a classification does her reaction show?

options.text: Prediction: she now knows how her problems will develop
Access to help: she can now get care and support
Acknowledgement that what she experiences is real and taken seriously
Explanation of why her problems developed and why they persist

l1.explanation: Lisa shows a useful function: recognition of suffering, the feeling that what she experiences has a name and is taken seriously. B is also a real function of a classification, but her words are about recognition, not about getting care. A is not something a classification does, and D is something it does not do either, because it only describes a pattern.

l1.question: Mark says: "Since I got the label, my family calls me 'the borderline'. Whenever I'm upset, they say it's my disorder." Which risk does this show most directly?

options.text: Stigma and reification: he is seen as the disorder
Symptom heterogeneity: people with the label differ strongly
Diagnostic comorbidity: he now also has a second label
Weak validity: the label does not predict his treatment

l1.explanation: His family sees him as "the disorder" (stigma), treats the disorder as a thing that causes all his feelings (reification), and no longer sees his upset as an understandable reaction (loss of context). B, C and D are other limitations of categories, but none of them is shown in his family's reaction.

l1.question: A psychologist discusses a classification with a client. Which approach fits Lecture 1 best?

options.text: Walk through the criteria one by one, to show the fit.
Present it as a working hypothesis, to drop soon after intake.
Postpone it until treatment starts, so it cannot bias the client.
Describe it as a pattern linked to the client's own story.

l1.explanation: Validate the experience, describe the classification as a pattern and not as who someone is, link it to the client's story, context and strengths, and explain that it is a tool that opens doors, not the full picture. A treats the criteria list as the whole message, B makes the classification disappear after intake, and C withholds a function that is useful.

l2.question: A school psychologist wants to know how often and for how long 9-year-old Daan leaves his seat during maths lessons. She sits at the back of the classroom with a tally sheet listing "out of seat" and records each episode and its duration. Which method is this?

options.text: Self-monitoring (self-report)
Hetero-anamnesis (interview)
Direct, (semi-)structured observation
Unstructured, indirect observation

l2.explanation: She decided in advance which behavior (out of seat) and which aspects (frequency, duration) to record = (semi-)structured; she watches it herself = direct. A is wrong: the client would record his own behavior. B is wrong: no informant is interviewed. D is wrong on both counts.

l2.question: Which WISC-V subtest counts toward a primary index but not toward the FSIQ?

options.text: Visual Puzzles
Figure Weights
Arithmetic
Coding

l2.explanation: The 10 primary subtests = the 7 FSIQ subtests + Visual Puzzles, Picture Span, Symbol Search. Figure Weights (B) and Coding (D) are FSIQ subtests. Arithmetic (C) is a secondary subtest — it counts for neither the FSIQ nor a primary index.

l2.question: Which statement about the WAIS-IV is NOT correct?

options.text: The FSIQ is based on the 10 core WAIS subtests.
Figure Weights is a supplemental subtest of Perceptual Reasoning Index.
Arithmetic is a core subtest of the Working Memory Index.
Information is a supplemental Verbal Comprehension subtest; Comprehension is core.

l2.explanation: In the WAIS-IV, Information is core (VCI = Similarities, Vocabulary, Information) and Comprehension is supplemental. A, B and C are all correct. Watch out: in the WISC-V, Figure Weights is a primary FSIQ subtest and Arithmetic is secondary (FRI) — the two batteries differ.

l2.question: A client's Perceptual Reasoning Index is 91 (27th percentile, 95% CI 84–99). Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The client answered about 27% of the perceptual reasoning items correctly on the test.
The client scored at or above 27% of peers; the true score likely lies 84–99.
There is a 95% chance that the client's observed score is exactly 91 points.
The score is a relative weakness, because it is below the average of 100.

l2.explanation: A percentile compares with people (the norm group), not with items (A). The CI is about the true score, not the observed score — the observed score is simply 91 (C). A "relative weakness" is judged against the person's own mean (MIS/FSIQ) with a critical value, not against 100 (D). Also: 91 falls in the Average range (90–109).

l2.question:
I. A statistically significant difference between two index scores means that the difference is rare in the norm group.
II. A large difference that occurs frequently in the norm group is less diagnostically specific.

options.text: Only II is correct
Only I is correct
Both are correct
Both are incorrect

l2.explanation: I is wrong: "significant" only means the difference is bigger than expected from measurement error; whether it is rare is a separate question answered by the base rate (confusing the two = interpretation error 05). II is literally on the slide: a large profile difference may occur frequently and is therefore less diagnostically specific.

l2.question: A 10-year-old starts WISC-V Similarities at the entry item for her age and answers the first two items incorrectly. What does the manual require?

options.text: Discontinue the subtest, because she has two zero scores at the start.
Continue forward and correct the score afterwards with the age norm table.
Apply the reversal rule: go back until the required consecutive correct responses.
Apply the start rule at the next session, starting at item 1.

l2.explanation: The starting level has not been established → go back to easier items (slide example: first two items after the entry item incorrect → go back). The discontinue rule (A) applies after a predetermined number of consecutive zeros (e.g., three) once testing is under way. B and D are not standardized procedures.

l2.question: Which WISC-V subtest has no strict time limit?

options.text: Figure Weights
Similarities
Arithmetic
Visual Puzzles

l2.explanation: Timed subtests: Block Design, Coding, Figure Weights, Visual Puzzles, Symbol Search, Cancellation, Arithmetic. For untimed subtests such as Similarities, allow about 30 seconds per item and, if needed, ask "Do you know the answer?"

l2.question: A researcher notes that all cognitive tasks in her study correlate positively, and argues that any sufficiently diverse set of tasks will estimate the same general factor. Which two concepts from Spearman does she use?

options.text: The general g-factor and specific s-factor
Fluid and crystallized intelligence factors
The operations, contents and products
Positive manifold and indifference of indicator

l2.explanation: Positive manifold = tasks correlate positively (empirical basis for g). Indifference of the indicator = different sets of tasks approximate the same g, provided they are cognitively diverse. A names the two factors but not these two ideas. B is Cattell/Horn (CHC). C is Guilford.

l2.question: Which statement about Thurstone is correct?

options.text: He rejected g, but his primary mental abilities turned out to be positively correlated.
He described 120 abilities from combinations of operations, contents and products in one model.
He placed g at the top, with verbal-educational and visuospatial-mechanical group factors below it.
His model is the most empirically supported and underlies the WISC and WAIS.

l2.explanation: Thurstone's 7 primary mental abilities were meant to be independent, but they correlate positively — his limitation. B = Guilford (5 × 4 × 6 = 120). C = Vernon. D = CHC.

l2.question: A client is asked to recall a story that was read to her 20 minutes earlier, and to name as many animals as possible in one minute. Which CHC broad ability do both tasks mainly tap?

options.text: Gsm — short-term memory capacity
Gc — crystallized intelligence and knowledge
Glr — long-term storage and retrieval
Gs — cognitive processing speed

l2.explanation: Glr = storing information for longer periods and retrieving it efficiently when needed (delayed recall; fluent retrieval of words). Gsm (A) is holding information for a few seconds. Gc (B) is breadth of knowledge (knowing what an animal is), not retrieving fast. Gs (D) is speed on simple visual/cognitive tasks like Coding.

l2.question: A 12-year-old's WISC-V profile: VCI 124, VSI 96, FRI 101, WMI 82, PSI 79. The differences are reliable and rare. How should the FSIQ be reported, according to the lecture?

options.text: "The FSIQ is invalid because the index scores differ too much from each other."
Leave the FSIQ out of the report and only report the separate subtest scores.
Report the FSIQ as the most accurate single estimate of the child's overall intelligence.
"The FSIQ is a summary score to be interpreted cautiously; domain scores matter more."

l2.explanation: "Don't throw it away, but contextualize!" The slide says never write "the FSIQ is invalid" (A) and warns against disregarding the FSIQ as soon as indices differ (B, error 03). C ignores that a strongly disharmonic profile qualifies the global score.

l2.question: You consider using a new test to decide about school placement. You ask: "What evidence supports this interpretation and this decision?" Which quality criterion is this?

options.text: Norms
Validity
Reliability
Basic principles

l2.explanation: Validity = evidence that supports the interpretation and decision. Norms (A) = is the norm group appropriate. Reliability (C) = size of measurement error. Basic principles (D) = are construct, aim and intended use explicitly defined — close, but that is about the definition, not the evidence.

l2.question: A psychologist assesses a recently arrived refugee with limited Dutch using Raven's Progressive Matrices. Which report sentence fits the lecture best?

options.text: "Because a non-verbal test was used, the result is free of cultural influence."
"The result gives a complete and reliable picture of the client's cognitive profile."
"Language demands were reduced; influences of education and test-taking experience were not eliminated."
"Because the test is non-verbal, the choice of norm group is not important."

l2.explanation: "Lower language demands do not mean culture-free": state that language demands were reduced, not that cultural influences were eliminated (A = error 08). Non-verbal tests have narrower domain coverage than full batteries (B). Test-taking experience, education, visual conventions, speed, motivation, instructions and the norm group remain relevant (D).

l2.question: A 45-year-old woman with a severe depressive episode takes the WAIS-IV. Her PSI is 78; her other indices are around 100. What is the most appropriate first thought?

options.text: Consider psychomotor slowing from depression, medication, fatigue and graphomotor skills before concluding.
Conclude that she has a lasting processing-speed deficit that explains her depression.
Conclude that the FSIQ is invalid and should not be reported anywhere.
Conclude that she was not motivated, because the PSI mainly reflects effort.

l2.explanation: For low PSI the slide lists: visual scanning, graphomotor skills, psychomotor slowing due to depression, medication, pain and fatigue (also: suboptimal validity makes scores less informative). B makes a causal claim and treats IQ as fixed. C: never call the FSIQ invalid. D: PSI is "not equivalent to general slowness, lack of motivation, or lack of understanding".

l2.question: Which examiner behavior violates standardized WISC-V administration?

options.text: Saying "You're working really hard" after the child struggles with a difficult item.
Asking "Can you tell me a little more about that?" after an unclear answer.
Letting the child briefly finish a Block Design item after the time limit.
Saying "Yes, well done, that's right!" after each correct answer to motivate the child.

l2.explanation: Standardized responding = praise effort, not correctness. Saying "that's right" gives feedback on the content and changes the conditions compared with the norm group. A is an allowed encouragement; B is allowed probing for unclear/incomplete answers; C is what the slide recommends (don't stop abruptly, only score within the limit).

l2.question: Noor is tested on 9 October 2026. Her date of birth is 23 December 2012. What is her chronological age, and which Wechsler test fits her?

options.text: 13 years, 10 months, 16 days: WISC-V
13 years, 9 months, 16 days: WAIS-IV
13 years, 9 months, 16 days: WISC-V
13 years, 10 months, 16 days: WAIS-IV

l2.explanation: Subtract year-month-day: 9 days minus 23 is impossible, so borrow a month (39 - 23 = 16 days); 9 months minus 12 is impossible, so borrow a year (21 - 12 = 9 months); 2025 - 2012 = 13. The age 13;9;16 falls in the WISC-V range (6:0-16:11), while the WAIS-IV starts at 16. Forgetting the month borrow gives 10 months, and rounding up is never allowed: use the norm table for her exact age.

l2.question: A child has these WISC-V primary index scores: VCI 98, VSI 104, FRI 110, WMI 84, PSI 99. What is the MIS (mean index score)?

options.text: 99, the average of all five indices
103, the average without the lowest index
97, the midpoint of highest and lowest index
104, the average of the three highest indices

l2.explanation: The MIS is the mean of the five primary indices: (98 + 104 + 110 + 84 + 99) / 5 = 495 / 5 = 99. Dropping the lowest index, taking the midpoint of the extremes, or averaging only the highest indices does not give the child's own average.

l2.question: The child has VCI 98, VSI 104, FRI 110, WMI 84 and PSI 99 (MIS = 99). The critical value is 10 points (invented). Which indices are candidate strengths or weaknesses?

options.text: VSI is a candidate strength; WMI is a candidate weakness
FRI and VSI are candidate strengths; WMI is a candidate weakness
FRI is a candidate strength; VCI is a candidate weakness
FRI is a candidate strength; WMI is a candidate weakness

l2.explanation: Each index is compared with the MIS: VCI -1, VSI +5, FRI +11, WMI -15, PSI 0. Only FRI (+11) and WMI (-15) go beyond the critical value of 10. VSI at +5 and VCI at -1 are within it.

l2.question: A child's WMI (84) is 15 points below the MIS (99), beyond the critical value. Which two checks must follow before writing "relative weakness in working memory" in the report?

options.text: The overall reliability of the WMI, and the fit with the FSIQ
The base rate of such a gap, and the fit with complaints
The size of the critical value, and the fit with the MIS
The test-retest reliability of the WMI, and the norm group's size

l2.explanation: Three questions apply to every difference: significant (yes, beyond the critical value), unusual (look up the base rate in the norm group) and relevant (does it fit the complaints, observations, history and school functioning). Only after these should the finding be written as a hypothesis, with its uncertainty.

l2.question: A report says: "Tom has a poor working memory (WMI = 78) and will therefore always struggle at school." Which set of problems does this sentence contain?

options.text: A label, a score without interval, a causal claim, a norm error
A label, a score with interval, a causal claim, a fixed prediction
A label, a score without interval, a causal claim, a fixed prediction
A label, a score without interval, a rare pattern, a fixed prediction

l2.explanation: The sentence uses a label ("poor") instead of a description, gives a point estimate without a confidence interval, makes a causal claim ("therefore"), predicts a fixed future ("always"), and does not link the score to observations or daily life. The other sets add a norm error, an interval or a rare pattern, none of which this sentence contains.

l2.question: Which rewrite of "Tom has a poor working memory (WMI = 78) and will therefore always struggle at school" fits the lecture best?

options.text: On tasks needing spoken information to be held, he scored lower (WMI 78, 95% CI 72-87), matching his teacher's report from class.
On tasks needing spoken information to be held, he scored lower (WMI 78, 95% CI 72-87), which indicates a working memory disorder.
On tasks needing spoken information to be held, he scored lower (WMI 78, 95% CI 72-87), which explains his problems in class.
On tasks needing spoken information to be held, he scored lower (WMI 78, 95% CI 72-87), so he will probably need support.

l2.explanation: A good sentence describes what he did on the tasks, gives the score with its confidence interval, links it to observations and the teacher's report, and offers a tentative interpretation for daily life. The others claim a disorder, state a cause, or predict the future.

l2.question: The school asks about Amira (11, arrived from Syria 14 months ago, speaks Arabic and basic Dutch): "Does she have a learning disability or is she still learning the language?" What is the right starting point for choosing instruments?

options.text: The target group: her age, language and schooling
The referral question and the purpose of the assessment
The construct coverage: which abilities the tests measure
The norm group: its size, recency and representativeness

l2.explanation: Start from the referral question, not from the test on the shelf: here the purpose is to separate learning ability from language exposure. Then check the target group (age, limited Dutch, different schooling), the construct coverage and the norm group. Each of those is a later check, not the starting point.

l2.question: For Amira (11, limited Dutch), a psychologist considers the WISC-V. Which part is hardest to interpret for her, and why?

options.text: FRI, because Matrix Reasoning and Figure Weights depend on school experience
WMI, because Digit Span depends on hearing and repeating Dutch numbers
PSI, because Coding and Symbol Search depend on familiarity with timed tests
VCI, because Similarities and Vocabulary depend on Dutch and cultural knowledge

l2.explanation: Verbal Comprehension subtests rely heavily on Dutch and on culturally acquired knowledge, so a low VCI would be hard to interpret: it could reflect language exposure rather than ability. Fluid-reasoning, working-memory and speed tasks depend much less on Dutch, so they can be interpreted more cautiously.

l2.question: Which assessment plan fits the case of Amira (11, limited Dutch) best?

options.text: A non-verbal test, parent and interpreter interviews, and a later repeat
The full WISC-V with a live interpreter translating every single item
A non-verbal test only, with Dutch norms and one short session
The full WISC-V in Dutch, with extra time on every task

l2.explanation: The plan combines a non-verbal test (for example Raven's) or the less language-heavy WISC-V indices with hetero-anamnesis through an interpreter, school records, classroom observation, and preferably a repeated assessment later. A single assessment is rarely enough, non-verbal does not mean culture-free, and an improvised translation or extra time breaks standardisation.

l2.question: Before interpreting the scores of a child from another country, a psychologist runs a fairness check. Which question belongs to it?

options.text: Which subtests, such as Vocabulary or Coding, have the highest reliability?
Which scores, such as FSIQ or MIS, would rise after more practice?
Which alternative explanations, such as limited schooling or trauma, are possible?
Which examiner, such as a senior colleague, should score the protocol?

l2.explanation: The fairness check asks: is the norm group appropriate, do instructions depend on the language, do items rely on culturally acquired knowledge, what alternative explanations exist (limited schooling, trauma, test unfamiliarity), and what extra information or adapted procedure is needed. The other questions are about psychometrics or the examiner, not fairness.

l2.question: A mini-report says: "Sven's Coding scaled score of 6 shows that he has ADHD." What is wrong with this sentence?

options.text: A significant difference is confused with rarity, without any base rate
A subtest score is compared with the MIS, not the norm group
A scaled score of 6 is called low, but it is average
A single subtest score is treated as proof of an ADHD diagnosis

l2.explanation: A single low subtest score cannot show ADHD, and the WISC-V is not a diagnostic instrument for ADHD: a low Coding score has many possible explanations (motor speed, fatigue, anxiety, attention). A scaled score of 6 is below the mean of 10, so it is low. The other options describe errors that this sentence does not contain.

l2.question: A mini-report says: "The test used norms from 1995." What is the main consequence for interpreting Sven's scores?

options.text: Scores are probably underestimated because of the Flynn effect
Scores are probably overestimated because of the Flynn effect
Scores are probably unchanged because norms affect only reliability
Scores are probably underestimated because older norm groups scored higher

l2.explanation: Outdated norms mean the norm group scored lower than people do today (the Flynn effect: rising scores over time), so the client's scores are probably overestimated. The psychologist should check the norming year and report this as a limitation. Norm age does not leave scores unchanged, and because older norm groups scored lower, the error pushes scores up, not down.

l2.question: A 34-year-old engineer (WAIS-IV) has VCI 113 and PRI 91. The 22-point gap exceeds the critical value and occurs in 8% of the norm group. Since a concussion he struggles with technical drawings. How should the gap be treated?

options.text: Significant but fairly common, so no further assessment is needed
Significant and rare, so strong evidence of brain damage
Significant, fairly unusual and relevant: a hypothesis to test further
Significant and unusual, so the FSIQ is invalid entirely

l2.explanation: Apply the three questions: significant (beyond the critical value), unusual (8% of the norm group is fairly rare) and relevant (the gap fits his new trouble with technical drawings). That supports a hypothesis for further assessment, after checking validity such as fatigue or motor problems. It is never a diagnosis by itself, and the FSIQ is a summary to interpret with caution.

l3.question: Client: "Everything is going wrong at home." Psychologist: "Can you describe a specific moment this week when things went wrong at home?" Which skill does the psychologist use?

options.text: Paraphrasing
Nuancing empathy
Concretizing
Verbal following

l3.explanation: "Everything" is a red-flag word; asking for a specific moment is the practical concretizing question from the slide. A paraphrase would restate the content ("Things at home are hard right now"). Nuancing empathy offers a new link tentatively. Verbal following ("mm-hm, go on") adds no direction — this question clearly steers towards a concrete event, so it's selective, not non-selective.

l3.question:
Consider the two statements about unconditional positive appreciation.
I. It means the practitioner approves of the client's behaviour, provided that the behaviour is understandable from the client's history.
II. A diagnostic attitude in line with it asks: "What has made this behaviour understandable for this client?"

options.text: Only statement II is correct
Only statement I is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

l3.explanation: Statement I is the classic trap: acceptance is not unconditional approval — understanding where behaviour comes from doesn't mean approving it. You take the client's intentions seriously (e.g. the overprotective parent). Statement II is the exact diagnostic attitude from the slide.

l3.question: A client feels ashamed that she can't make choices without asking her sister first. Which self-disclosure by the psychologist best meets all four checks from the lecture?

options.text: "I recognise that so well. I called my mother for every decision; let me tell you how I stopped…"
"Honestly, I'm quite tired today myself, so I really understand that deciding things can be hard for you too."
"I have the same thing, and to be honest it's probably a lot worse for me than for you."
"I also sometimes find it hard to decide without asking someone. What is it like for you to choose alone?"

l3.explanation: D is functional (reduces shame, changes her perception of the problem), relevant (same theme), measured (one sentence, not more intimate than the client) and returns the focus with a question. A fails "measured" and "return the focus" (long story about the practitioner). B isn't relevant (tiredness ≠ dependence on others) and is about the practitioner's state. C makes it about the practitioner and isn't helpful for the client.

l3.question: To create calm, a psychologist leaves a long silence at the start of an intake. The client grows visibly anxious, fidgets and doesn't dare to begin. What is the best next step according to the lecture?

options.text: Keep allowing the silence, because calm and safety need time to build up.
"It's hard to start. Could you tell me about a recent difficult moment?"
"What is the problem that brings you here today, in your own words?"
Briefly explain how anxiety works, to help put the client more at ease.

l3.explanation: This is option C from the in-class case. The silence is not working for this client, so you adjust: naming what's happening lowers the pressure, and a concrete entry point makes starting easy. A keeps doing what makes the client anxious. C questions more forcefully (the slide's option A) → feels like an interrogation. D is the teacher role far too early and fills the space with your own content.

l3.question: A psychologist says: "Could it be that skipping the supermarket gives you relief in the short run, but makes the fear bigger in the long run?" Which practitioner role is this primarily?

options.text: Trusted figure
Teacher
Communicative detective
Coach

l3.explanation: The teacher tentatively offers a different perspective — this is almost literally the slide's "offer tentatively" avoidance example. The detective explores and explains why they ask; the coach turns insight into action (can/dare/plan/follow-up); the trusted figure offers calm and space without new content.

l3.question: Client: "I now see that I avoid my manager. I know exactly what I'd want to ask her, but I'm scared she'll think I'm incompetent." Before sending the client "onto the field", which coach check is most clearly the problem here?

options.text: Can — does the client have the skill needed?
Plan — is the step small enough to achieve?
Follow-up — when will we evaluate this next step?
Dare — is there enough confidence in their ability?

l3.explanation: He knows exactly what to ask (so "can" is fine) but is afraid → the issue is confidence ("dare"). You might role-play first or make the step smaller. "Plan" and "follow-up" still need attention, but nothing in the vignette signals they are the main obstacle.

l3.question: Which statement about paraphrasing, reflecting and summarizing is NOT correct?

options.text: A reflection mainly restates the factual content, whereas a paraphrase names the underlying feeling.
A summary can be used at a topic transition and at the next conversation's start.
After each of the three, the practitioner checks with the client: "Is that right?"
A reflection may name a feeling the client did not mention, such as fear.

l3.explanation: A paraphrase focuses on content; a reflection on feeling/meaning. B is correct (timing: confusion, closure, transition, start of next conversation). C is on the slide. D is correct — the slide's reflection adds "perhaps also afraid that you are losing control", which the client never said.

l3.question: Client: "Just tell me what I should do. That's what you're here for." According to the seven-step guide for clarifying the situation, what should the psychologist do first?

options.text: Name the misunderstanding: "I notice you expect a solution from me."
Explain what you will not do: "I won't give advice yet."
Show understanding for the client's wish to get a solution quickly.
Make an agreement together about how to proceed during today's session.

l3.explanation: Order: 1 show understanding → 2 name the misunderstanding → 3 what I don't want + why → 4 what I do want + why → 5 receive the response → 6 make an agreement → 7 return to the conversation. A is step 2, B step 3, D step 6.

l3.question: Five minutes into a first intake, a client talks about conflicts with his boss. The psychologist calmly says: "I hear a lot about difficult bosses. At the same time, I hear little about your own part. Could there be something there as well?" How should this be evaluated according to the lecture?

options.text: Good: confronting is a selective listening skill that fits well in the first phase of the conversation.
Good: because it is calm and hypothetical, a confrontation like this can be used at any moment.
Wrong: confrontation is aggressive by nature and has no place in psychological assessment or in intake conversations.
Well-phrased but probably too early: confronting is a nuancing skill for the second phase, once safety exists.

l3.explanation: The wording is exactly the slide's good example (calm, hypothetical, accepting). But timing is a skill: in the first phase you connect with the client's frame of reference (listen, reflect, summarize); confronting belongs to the nuancing skills, used "only later", when the relationship can tolerate a new perspective. A is wrong twice (not selective listening, not first phase). B ignores timing. C is wrong: confrontation done well is a legitimate skill.

l3.question: "We have 45 minutes. I suggest we first clarify together what is going on, and then look at what is needed. Is that okay with you? Are there things you definitely want to discuss?" To which family of interviewing skills does this belong?

options.text: Non-selective listening skills
Regulating skills
Selective listening skills
Nuancing skills

l3.explanation: This is the slide's initial-contract script: agreements about time, goal, roles and the client's expectations. Regulating skills give clarity about how the conversation proceeds. The question at the end is open, but its function is structuring, not exploring the story (selective listening).

l3.question:
Consider the two statements.
I. Even a restrained psychologist who mostly says "mm-hm" influences what the client ends up talking about.
II. Because attention is never neutral, a psychologist should avoid responding selectively to specific parts of the client's story.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

l3.explanation: I = the slide "attention is never neutral": presence encourages talking in general, and what you respond to gets more space. II draws the wrong conclusion: the lecture wants you to consciously choose what to follow (selective listening skills; "a practitioner consciously chooses when to follow") — not to avoid selecting.

l3.question: Client: "I've been drinking quite a lot lately. And things at home aren't going very well either." Which response is an example of nuancing empathy?

options.text: "It sounds as though things at home are hard and leave you with little peace."
"So you are drinking more because of the tension at home. Is that right?"
"I wonder whether drinking and tension at home reinforce each other. What do you think?"
"Do you have any idea what has made you start drinking more often lately?"

l3.explanation: C makes a new connection and keeps a questioning tone, so the client can correct it — that's nuancing empathy (slide). A is (basic) empathy: it stays with what the client said. B states an interpretation as a fact (assumption, no room to correct). D is the softened why-question — an open exploring question (selective listening), not nuancing.

l3.question: Which rewrite of "Why do you always cancel your appointments?" best invites exploration instead of justification?

options.text: "I noticed a few appointments were cancelled. Why was coming difficult on those days?"
"I noticed a few appointments were cancelled. What made coming difficult on those days?"
"I noticed you often cancel. What is the main reason you cancel so often?"
"I noticed a few appointments were cancelled. How come you did not call earlier?"

l3.explanation: B drops the red-flag word "always", states a neutral observation and asks a curious "what" question about circumstances. A keeps the "why" that invites justification. C generalises ("often") and asks for a reason. D is a hidden accusation about the client's behaviour.

l3.question: Which rewrite of "Why are you so angry at your sister?" uses reflection plus concretizing?

options.text: "It sounds like you carry much anger towards your sister. Is that right?"
"Can you describe a recent moment when you felt angry at your sister?"
"It sounds like you are angry. Can you explain why you feel this way?"
It sounds like much anger towards your sister. Can you describe a recent moment?

l3.explanation: D first reflects the feeling without judgement and then asks for a concrete recent moment. A reflects but stays abstract. B concretizes but skips the reflection. C reflects briefly but then asks a disguised "why" question.

l3.question: Client: "Everything is a mess at work lately, it never goes right." Besides asking for a specific moment, which question best checks the word "never"?

options.text: "Was there a moment recently when it did go reasonably well?"
"Why do you think it never goes right for you at work?"
"What would have to change for things to go right at work?"
"Which colleague makes it go wrong most often at your work?"

l3.explanation: "Never" is a red flag, so you look for an exception. A does that without arguing. B is a why-question that invites justification. C jumps to solutions before the problem is concrete. D looks for someone to blame and is not a check on "never".

l3.question: A client says: "Since my mother moved into a nursing home, I visit her every day after work. I'm too tired to cook or call friends, and I feel guilty when I skip a visit." Which response is a reflection?

options.text: "You visit your mother every day after work, which leaves you no energy for cooking or friends."
"If I understand correctly: you visit daily, you are exhausted, and skipping feels guilty. Is that right?"
"You feel torn: exhausted from the daily visits, yet guilty as soon as you take time for yourself."
"Perhaps you could visit less often, so that you have the energy for cooking and friends again."

l3.explanation: A reflection names the feeling behind the content (torn, tired, guilty). A is a paraphrase (content only). B is a summary (overview plus check). D is advice, which is a solution reflex and not an interviewing skill of this kind.

l3.question: The same client has told you about the daily visits, the tiredness, the neglected friends and the guilt. Which response is a good summary?

options.text: You are a loving daughter, so your guilt is understandable. Is that right?
So you visit daily, you are exhausted, friends wait, you feel guilty. Right?
You feel both exhausted and guilty, which is a strain. Is that right?
You go daily, which is why you cannot cook or call. Is that right?

l3.explanation: A summary gives an overview of several points, checks it ("Is that right?") and can lead to a choice of what to look at first. A reassures and interprets. C is a reflection of feeling only. D is a paraphrase of a single part of the story.

l3.question: During the seven-step guide, the psychologist has just said what she does want: "I'd like us to first understand together what is going on." What is the next step?

options.text: Suggest an agreement: "Shall we use today to get a clear picture?"
Return to the conversation: "Can you tell me about the last time?"
Name the misunderstanding: "I notice that you mainly expect some advice from me."
Receive the response and listen: "How is that for you to hear now?"

l3.explanation: After explaining what you do want and why, you let the client respond and listen (and reflect any irritation). Then comes the agreement (A), and last the return to the conversation (B). Naming the misunderstanding (C) is an earlier step.

l3.question: First session: a client arrives shaking, with tears in her eyes, and says "I don't know if I can talk about this." Which role and response fit best?

options.text: Trusted figure: stay calm, give space, and let her set the pace.
Teacher: normalise her fear, and explain why talking about it can help.
Detective: gently ask what exactly feels too difficult to say out loud.
Coach: agree a small step, such as writing down a first sentence.

l3.explanation: She needs safety, calm and space, so the trusted figure fits: tolerate the emotion and let her decide the pace. The teacher (B) offers new perspectives, which is too early. The detective (C) asks for information and adds pressure. The coach (D) turns insight into behaviour, but she has no insight task yet.

l3.question: You need to know about a client's relationship, but he looks surprised when you ask about his partner. Which role and response fit best?

options.text: Trusted figure: stay silent and wait until he decides to talk about it himself.
Teacher: tentatively suggest that his relationship is probably the cause of his problem.
Detective: explain that stress at home can affect sleep, and ask for his permission.
Coach: check whether he can, dares and plans to talk about his relationship.

l3.explanation: The communicative detective makes clear why a question is asked, links it to the complaint and asks permission. A leaves him confused. B offers an explanation without basis. D is for turning insight into action, which is not the issue here.

l4.question: Mr. De Vries (42) has had panic attacks for months. His company doctor advises him to have a psychological assessment. His wife phones the practice to make the appointment. His employer formally requests and pays for the assessment and wants to hear whether he is fit for work. Who is the referring party?

options.text: The company doctor
The employer
The wife
Mr. De Vries

l4.explanation: The referring party is whoever first contacts the care provider, and the wife made the phone call. The company doctor is the referrer (professional advice, A). The employer is the commissioning party and also an involved party (B). Mr. De Vries is the client (D).

l4.question:
Consider these statements.
I. One person can hold several formal roles at once. For example, a GP can be both the referrer and the referring party.
II. The referrer is the person who formally commissions the psychological assessment.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

l4.explanation: I is correct: in the Jorna case the GP both advises (referrer) and phones (referring party). II is wrong: the commissioning party formally commissions the assessment. The referrer is the professional who advised the client about the importance of assessment.

l4.question: Which statement about the diagnostic cycle of De Bruyn et al. (2003) is NOT correct?

options.text: The many arrows show that you can return to an earlier phase when new information appears.
The cycle ends with the advice (feedback) session, after which a new therapy cycle can start.
Working with the model also helps limit the influence of the availability heuristic and confirmation bias.
Each phase must be fully completed before the next one starts, so the cycle is linear.

l4.explanation: The arrows go both ways and include shortcuts. The cycle is flexible and iterative, so D is the incorrect statement. A, B and C are all taken from the lecture: back-steps, the end at Adv followed by the therapy cycle, and "a model helps discipline clinical intuition" against these two biases.

l4.question: A client says: "My boss sent me an e-mail late at night. I immediately thought I'd be fired. I felt sick with fear, so I called in sick the next day. Now I'm even further behind at work." Which 5G mapping is correct?

options.text: Event: "I thought I'd be fired" · Behaviour: called in sick · Consequence: further behind at work
Event: late-night e-mail · Thought: "I'll be fired" · Behaviour: called in sick · Consequence: further behind
Event: late-night e-mail · Thought: "I'll be fired" · Behaviour: further behind · Consequence: called in sick
Event: late-night e-mail · Feeling: "I'll be fired" · Behaviour: called in sick · Consequence: further behind

l4.explanation: Event = what happened (the e-mail). Thought = what went through the mind ("I'll be fired"). Feeling = sick with fear. Behaviour = what he did (called in sick). Consequence = what happened next (further behind). A turns a thought into the event. C swaps behaviour and consequence. D labels a thought as a feeling, which is the classic 5G mistake.

l4.question: A 16-year-old is sent for assessment by the juvenile court. In the first session he says everything is fine and that he used cannabis "once or twice". Two sessions later, when he trusts the psychologist more, he talks about daily use. Which pair of concepts from the lecture both apply?

options.text: Coerced referral and gradual disclosure
Overreporting and voluntary referral
Underreporting and anchoring bias
Gradual disclosure and overreporting

l4.explanation: Pressure from the justice system = coerced, which lowers openness. The truth coming out as trust grows = gradual disclosure. He does also underreport at first, but C pairs that with anchoring, which is a clinician's reasoning error and not something the client does. B and D contain overreporting (exaggerating), which is the opposite of what happens.

l4.question: On the referral call, a woman hesitantly mentions "a difficult past" she doesn't want to go into. Later she says she "sometimes thinks everyone would be better off without her". According to the lecture, what is the best approach?

options.text: Respect her pace on both topics, and ask about them only in the intake once trust has really grown.
Ask directly and in detail about her past now, because complaints should always be explored directly at the referral.
End the call and refer her to a crisis service without questions, because risk is not part of referral.
Don't push for details about her past, but do ask directly about suicidal thoughts and whether she is safe.

l4.explanation: Trauma and shame call for careful pacing (consent, choice, pace). Suicidality always calls for a direct question. A wrongly delays the safety question. B violates the pacing rule: "always directly" is exactly the statement the lecture rejects. C skips the assessment of safety that the lecture asks for ("I do want to assess whether you are safe today").

l4.question: Which statement about the complaint analysis is NOT correct?

options.text: The client's own language and beliefs are central, including what remains incomplete or unclear.
Its outcome is a clarifying diagnosis: an organised overview of the complaints and help-seeking questions.
Its aim is an objective identification of the problem with the help of classification systems.
A complaint can be a thought, feeling, behaviour or event that the client finds limiting.

l4.explanation: The slide says literally: "no objective identification". Going from subjective to objective and using classification systems is the problem analysis (Lecture 7). A, B and D are the slide's own descriptions of the complaint analysis and of a complaint.

l4.question: The referral letter says a boy "probably has ADHD". In the intake, the psychologist mainly asks about concentration and restlessness, and hardly asks about the recent divorce the parents mention. Later, the teacher reports that the problems only began after the divorce, but the psychologist keeps ADHD as the working idea with barely any change. Which two errors are shown, in this order?

options.text: Solution reflex, then premature explanation
Confirmation bias, then anchoring
Availability heuristic, then solution reflex
Anchoring, then confirmation bias

l4.explanation: First he searches only for information that fits ADHD: confirmation bias. Then new information arrives and he does not adjust enough: anchoring. D has the right terms in the wrong order. No advice is given, so there is no solution reflex (A, C).

l4.question: Lisa (35) reads about burnout online. She phones a psychology practice herself, pays for the assessment herself, and asks that nobody else be informed. Which formal roles does Lisa hold?

options.text: Client and commissioning party
Client and referring party
Referring and involved party
Client, referrer and commissioning party

l4.explanation: The assessment is about her (client). She made the first contact (referring party). She formally orders and pays (commissioning party). There is no referrer, because a referrer gives advice within a professional relationship and a website is not that (B). "Involved party" means someone else who is informed of the outcome (C).

l4.question: A psychologist asks: "Why are you coming now and not six months ago? Did something happen recently?" and "Why did you choose our specialised clinic instead of your GP's mental health nurse?" Which part of the referral heuristic do these questions belong to?

options.text: When: timing
What: previous care
Who: informants
What: expectations

l4.explanation: On the slide, "When" = why now, crisis/urgency, why this institution (rather than a lower- or higher-intensity level of care). "Previous care" (B) asks what has already been tried and why it stopped. "Expectations" (D) asks what success would look like and what people fear.

l4.question:
Consider these statements.
I. At referral you collect brief, concise, basic information. In the complaint analysis the client's experience and story are central.
II. When time is short, a well-validated questionnaire can replace the complaint analysis.

options.text: Both statements are correct
Only statement II is correct
Only statement I is correct
Both statements are incorrect

l4.explanation: I matches the labels in the cycle diagram (Ref = brief, concise, basic information; CA = the client's experience and story are central). II is wrong: questionnaires are "a tool, not a substitute for the intake". They can screen, identify themes, structure the conversation and monitor progress, but they cannot replace the complaint analysis. Validity doesn't change that.

l4.question: In the complaint analysis, a client says: "I feel depressed." Which response fits the lecture's guidelines best?

options.text: "Why do you feel so depressed? What do you think is really causing it?"
"By 'depressed', do you mean low mood or emptiness? Could you give an example?"
"That sounds like a depressive disorder to me. How long have you had it?"
"What do you do about it? Do you exercise, sleep enough and see friends?"

l4.explanation: "Vague words are diagnostic opportunities." B uses the slide's own follow-up for "depressed" and asks for a concrete example. A uses a why-question as the first response (a don't). C uses jargon and gives a premature explanation. D asks three questions in one and already leans towards solutions.

l4.question: Ahmed is off sick; his employer (HR) requests and pays for an assessment. His girlfriend wants advice on how to support him, and she is included with her own help question. Who forms the client system?

options.text: Ahmed alone, because he is the only person being assessed
Ahmed and his girlfriend, because both take part in the assessment
Ahmed and his employer, because the employer commissions the report
Ahmed, his girlfriend and the employer, because all hear the outcome

l4.explanation: The client system is the client plus the people included with their own help question, so Ahmed and his girlfriend. The employer and the company doctor are involved parties (they hear the outcome), not part of the client system. A ignores that she has her own question.

l4.question: Ahmed's employer wants a report on whether he can return to work. Which professional check is most important before sharing information?

options.text: Check that the employer has asked a clear question and signed the commissioning agreement.
Check that the company doctor has approved the content of the report before release.
Check that the girlfriend and the employer have both consented to receive the results.
Check that Ahmed agreed to what is shared and only necessary information goes out.

l4.explanation: Consent and privacy (GDPR): Ahmed must know and agree, and you share only what is needed, such as work capacity, not his life story. A clear question and contract (A) are good practice but do not cover his consent. The doctor does not decide for the client (B). The girlfriend and employer are not entitled to the same information (C).

l4.question: In the same case, the employer wants Ahmed back at work. Why is this relevant for the assessment?

options.text: Ahmed may colour his answers, so the perspectives must be kept apart.
The employer's wish makes Ahmed's help question invalid, so it is dropped.
Ahmed will answer accurately, since the employer never sees his own answers.
The employer's question defines the final outcome, so it simply takes priority.

l4.explanation: The employer's interest can make Ahmed less open (underreporting) or more open (overreporting), so you separate the perspectives. His own help question stays valid (B), the employer does see an outcome and has a stake (C), and the commissioning party's question does not automatically take priority (D).

l4.question: A father says: "My son has problems at school." Which is the best first question to turn this vague complaint into a 5G chain?

options.text: "Why do you think your son has problems at school?"
"Which school problem does he have exactly, dyslexia or ADHD?"
"Can you describe a recent school moment when it went wrong?"
"What have you already tried to help him at school?"

l4.explanation: The chain starts with a concrete event: what happened exactly, when, where. A is a why-question that asks for an explanation. B jumps to labels (premature explanation, jargon). D asks for solutions before the problem is clear.

l4.question: In that chain, you want to know what went through the son's mind. What is the best way to get the thought?

options.text: Ask the son himself, since the father can only guess what he thought.
Ask the father, since he knows his son best and sees him daily.
Infer it from the behaviour, since thoughts follow from what he did.
Use the teacher's report instead, because the school observed the behaviour directly.

l4.explanation: Thoughts are only truly known by the person himself, so you ask the son later. The father's guess is useful but only a first idea (B). Inferring thoughts from behaviour is guessing (C). The teacher sees behaviour, not thoughts (D).

l4.question: Emma (15) skips school. She says: "I want my mum and the school to stop pressuring me." What kind of help-seeking question is this?

options.text: An explanation question: she wants to understand why she skips school.
An advice question: she wants advice on how to return to school.
An indication question: she wants to know which support is needed.
A change-in-environment wish: she wants the others to change, not herself.

l4.explanation: Emma wants others to change, like the cannabis example on the slide. It is not about understanding (A), advice for herself (B) or a professional indication (C). A good psychologist still takes her wish seriously.

l4.question: Emma's mother says: "I want to understand why Emma doesn't go to school anymore and how I can get her back there without fighting every morning." What kind of question is this?

options.text: An explanation plus indication question, phrased in professional language
An explanation plus advice question, phrased in her words
An advice plus change-in-environment question, phrased in her words
An indication plus change-in-environment question, phrased in professional language

l4.explanation: "Why" is an explanation question and "how can I" is an advice question, both in a parent's own words. Explanation plus indication (A) is the school counsellor's professional version. The mother is not mainly asking for an indication or for others to change (C, D).

l4.question: The school counsellor asks: "Which factors explain Emma's school absence, and what support is indicated to get her back to school?" What kind of question is this?

options.text: An explanation plus advice question, phrased in her words
An advice plus change-in-environment question, phrased in her words
An explanation plus indication question, phrased in professional language
An indication plus change-in-environment question, phrased in professional language

l4.explanation: "Which factors explain" is an explanation question and "what support is indicated" is an indication question, phrased in professional language. Advice in a parent's own words (A) is the mother's voice. B and D mix in a wish for change in the environment, which is Emma's voice.

l4.question: Emma, her mother and the school counsellor each have a different help question. What should the psychologist do?

options.text: Merge the three questions into one professionally phrased question and answer that.
Answer the adults' questions, since Emma's wish is no assessment question.
Start with Emma's question only and add the others if time allows.
Write each question in their own words, prioritise together and answer all.

l4.explanation: You distinguish the perspectives, write each help question in the person's own words, prioritise together and make sure the assessment answers all of them. Merging into one professional question loses the voices (A), dismissing Emma's wish ignores her perspective (B), and answering one voice first leaves the others out (C).

l4.question: Five minutes into the intake the psychologist says: "Have you tried going to bed at the same time every night?" Which pitfall is this?

options.text: Solution reflex: giving advice before the problem is properly understood
Premature explanation: reading the complaint immediately as a mental disorder
Confirmation bias: looking for information that fits the first idea
Anchoring: not adjusting the first idea after new information arrives

l4.explanation: Advice before the problem is understood is the solution reflex. There is no explanation or diagnosis here (B), no search for confirming information (C) and no new information that is ignored (D).

l4.question: A client says "I'm always tired" and the psychologist immediately answers: "That's typical of depression." Which pitfall is this?

options.text: Solution reflex: giving advice about what the client should do
Premature explanation: reading the complaint immediately as a disorder
Availability heuristic: choosing the explanation that comes easily to mind
Anchoring: not adjusting the first idea after new information arrives

l4.explanation: Explaining the complaint as a disorder (and in jargon) before exploring it is premature explanation. No advice is given (A). There is no sign the idea came from a recent, vivid experience (C), and no new information is ignored (D).

l4.question: A psychologist who just attended a workshop on trauma now sees trauma behind almost every complaint. Which heuristic is at work?

options.text: Confirmation bias: asking only questions that fit the first idea
Anchoring: not adjusting the first idea after new information
Availability heuristic: choosing the explanation that comes easily to mind
Premature explanation: reading the complaint immediately as a disorder

l4.explanation: A recent, vivid workshop makes trauma the explanation that comes to mind most easily: the availability heuristic. Confirmation bias (A) is about which questions you ask, anchoring (B) about adjusting after new information, and premature explanation (D) about explaining too early.

l7.question: Which statement best describes the move from the complaint analysis to the problem analysis?

options.text: From objective to subjective: the psychologist sets aside classifications and focuses on the client's own meaning.
From description to explanation: the psychologist now looks for the conditions that caused the client's complaints.
From subjective to objective: the complaints are described and ordered with classification systems and theoretical models.
From help question to indication: the psychologist decides which treatment fits the complaints of this client.

l7.explanation: CA formulates the client's story as complaints and help questions (subjective). PA applies knowledge of classification systems and theoretical models so the problems become part of a theory or classification (objective). A reverses the direction. B describes the step after PA (explanatory analysis). D describes the indication analysis.

l7.question:
Consider the two statements.
I. The preliminary case inventory builds on the complaint analysis and describes the problem behaviour in concrete situations, including its history of onset and course.
II. A general problem inventory is needed because the complaint analysis is based on the client's own experience and is therefore often incomplete.

options.text: Both statements are correct.
Only statement I is correct.
Only statement II is correct.
Both statements are incorrect.

l7.explanation: I lists the elements of the preliminary case inventory (builds on CA; internal/external problem behaviour; concrete situations; history of onset and course). II is the reason for the general problem inventory given on the slide: CA reflects the client's experience and is often incomplete, so missing information is added — often with (semi-)structured interviews.

l7.question: Tom (29) reports "panic attacks". During the problem analysis the psychologist checks the case inventory from an objectifying perspective. Which question fits this check best?

options.text: "What does it mean to you, as a person, that you get these attacks?"
"Which experiences in your childhood could explain why you are getting these attacks now?"
"What would you like us to help you with, concretely, during this assessment together?"
"When was your first and worst attack, and what do you do or avoid?"

l7.explanation: The objectifying check asks whether the behaviour is described concretely enough and whether there is enough information on intensity and frequency; the slide's panic example is exactly D. A explores meaning (complaint analysis). B looks for causes (explanatory analysis). C is the help-seeking question (complaint analysis).

l7.question: What is the correct order of the sub-steps of "ordering and labelling"?

options.text: Classify the disorder → cluster the problems into a category → group complaints that belong together.
Group the complaints that belong together → cluster them into a category → classify the disorder.
Cluster the complaints into a category → formulate explanatory hypotheses → classify the most likely disorder.
Group the complaints → test the classification with a questionnaire → cluster them into a category.

l7.explanation: The slide: (1) organise complaints into groups that belong together (low mood, sadness, thoughts of death, reduced activity), (2) cluster into a category (mood problems), (3) classify (depressive disorder). A is reversed (starting from the label = top-down, risk of confirmation bias). C inserts explanations, which belong to EA. D puts testing before clustering.

l7.question: Which of the following is <u>not</u> one of Rutter's (1975) criteria for judging the severity of a symptom or problem behaviour?

options.text: Whether the behaviour fits the client's (sub)cultural background and norms.
Whether at least five symptoms are present for two weeks.
Whether the behaviour occurs in one situation or several situations.
Whether the behaviour is specific to psychopathology in this person.

l7.explanation: Rutter's list: appropriate for age, persistent, recent or long-standing, frequent, specific to psychopathology, situation-specific, isolated or not, interference with other areas, psychosocial stress, sociocultural background. A, C and D are all on it. Don't mix up severity criteria (Rutter) with classification criteria (DSM).
