options.text: Stop the child exactly at the time limit, to keep the whole administration strictly standardised.
Let the child finish and score the item as correct if the design is finally right.
Let the child continue briefly, end the item gradually, and score only performance within the limit.
Give a small hint on the pattern so the child can finish the item in time.

te.explanation: Only performance within the time limit is scored. But stopping abruptly can demotivate the child, so preferably let them continue briefly and then end the item gradually. Hints are never allowed on content (standardised responding); B breaks the scoring rules.→ re-read Lecture 2

te.question: According to Lecture 2, what is a key limitation of the Wechsler index scores?

options.text: They are battery-specific operationalisations, not CHC factors.
They have no available norms for adults.
They only measure crystallised intelligence in practice.
They cannot be used with young children.

te.explanation: Strengths of the Wechsler family: extensive norms, clinical familiarity, coverage of several domains. Limitation: the indices are battery-specific operationalisations, not pure CHC factors. (And on the WISC-V each primary index rests on only 2 subtests — don't treat it as a full assessment of the domain.)→ re-read Lecture 2

te.question: Which note taken during a WISC-V administration follows the lecture's advice on observation?

options.text: “Has poor working memory, especially on Digit Span.”
“Requested repetition on Digit Span; counted on fingers.”
“Probably has ADHD, because he was so restless.”
“Was lazy and unmotivated on the timed tasks.”

te.explanation: “Observations are data”: observe descriptively (“what did I see?”), not interpretively (“he has poor working memory”). B records task understanding and strategy. A and D are interpretations; C turns an observation into a diagnosis — and the WISC-V is not a diagnostic instrument for ADHD.→ re-read Lecture 2

te.question: A client says: “My mother still calls me every day to check whether I've eaten. It drives me crazy, but I feel guilty if I don't answer.” Which response is a reflection of feeling (rather than a paraphrase)?

options.text: “You feel torn: irritated by calls, yet guilty when you don't answer.”
“Your mother calls you every day to check whether you've eaten yet.”
“How often does she call exactly, and at what time of day?”
“Why do you answer her calls at all if they annoy you?”

te.explanation: A reflection names the feeling/meaning behind the words. B is a paraphrase (content in your own words). C is a closed, concretising question. D is a why-question that can make the client feel she has to justify herself.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: I. Genuineness means expressing every thought and feeling you have during the session, without filtering.II. Process goals, such as building calm and trust, are mainly the client's responsibility.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

te.explanation: Both wrong. I: genuineness includes tactful spontaneity — respond naturally, but don't express every thought or emotion unfiltered. II: process goals are mainly the practitioner's responsibility; outcome goals (the desired change) are owned mainly by the client.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: A client says: “Just tell me what I should do, that's why I'm here.” In the seven-step guide for clarifying the situation, what comes directly after “show understanding”?

options.text: Make a clear agreement.
Name the misunderstanding explicitly.
Say what you want.
Return to the conversation.

te.explanation: Order: 1 show understanding → 2 name the misunderstanding → 3 what I don't want + why → 4 what I do want + why → 5 receive the response → 6 make an agreement → 7 return to the conversation.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: Which practitioner response is an example of positive relabeling?

options.text: “You say nobody likes you, but Jayden and Ruben invited you on holiday.”
“I hear a lot about difficult bosses, but little about your own part.”
“Your stubbornness also shows that you stand up for what you find right.”
“I notice that we often only get to the core quite late today.”

te.explanation: Positive relabeling gives problem behaviour a new, more constructive label (like “slowness = wanting to think things through”). A = confronting with strengths (makes an exception visible). B = confronting a discrepancy (calm, hypothetical). D = discussing a pattern when closing is difficult (regulating).→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: A psychologist says: “To get a clear picture, I'd also like to hear what actually happens when you and your partner disagree. Is it okay if we focus on that for a moment?” Which role and technique is this?

options.text: Teacher — interpreting the underlying pattern and explaining it.
Coach — checking whether the step is small enough.
Trusted figure — non-selective listening without steering the conversation.
Communicative detective — investigating by explaining why you ask.

te.explanation: The communicative detective does focused exploration and explains why: “I'm asking this because… + it helps us to… + is it okay if we focus on that?” Without the explanation the same question can feel like an interrogation.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: Which order of skills fits the lecture's “timing is a skill” message?

options.text: Interpret and confront first, before the client builds up defences; then listen.
First safety and space; then precision and organisation; later insight and direction.
First concretise and summarise, then create safety, then interpret and inform clients.
Nuancing skills should never be used in psychological assessment, only in therapy.

te.explanation: First → Then → Only later. Nuancing skills (interpreting, confronting, nuancing empathy) come in the second phase, when the relationship is strong enough for the client to tolerate a new perspective.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: Which of these is NOT one of the coach checks before you send a client “onto the field”?

options.text: Can: does the client already have the necessary skill?
Dare: is there enough confidence in their own ability?
Plan: is the step small enough to be achievable?
Insight: does the client understand where the problem comes from?

te.explanation: The four checks are Can? Dare? Plan? Follow-up? (When will we evaluate what happened?). Full insight into the origin isn't required before trying new behaviour — the coach role starts exactly when insight alone does not lead to action.→ re-read Lecture 3

te.question: Noor (16) is brought to the practice by her father, who made the phone call. Her school counsellor had advised the father to seek help because Noor has stopped eating lunch at school. Noor says she only came “because Dad forced me”. Who is the referrer?

options.text: Noor herself
The father
The school counsellor
The psychologist

te.explanation: The referrer is the professional who, within a professional relationship, advised the client about the importance of assessment → the school counsellor. The father is the referring party (first contact with the care provider). Noor is the client.→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: Same case (Noor). What should the psychologist be most alert to, and with which attitude?

options.text: Overreporting; confront Noor with her inconsistencies right away, before any rapport is built.
Underreporting due to coercion; be curious about the function of minimising, not moralising.
Gradual disclosure; postpone eating questions until trust is complete, despite possible medical risks.
Anchoring; accept the father's view of the situation as the most objective one.

te.explanation: A coerced referral affects openness → underreporting is likely. Clinical stance: be curious about the function of the distortion, don't moralise. C is wrong: when there is risk (e.g. severe weight loss) you always ask directly. D: you distinguish perspectives, you don't decide who is “right”.→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: What is the outcome of the complaint analysis called, and what does it contain?

options.text: A clarifying diagnosis: organised overview of complaints and questions.
An explanatory diagnosis: the accepted and the rejected hypotheses.
A classification: the DSM disorder that fits best overall.
An indication: the treatment that fits the client best.

te.explanation: Complaint analysis → clarifying diagnosis (organisation of complaints and help questions). Classification belongs to the problem analysis; the explanatory diagnosis (integrative formulation) to the explanatory analysis; the indication to the indication analysis.→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: A client says: “The girl next door quickly looks away when I meet her on the street. Apparently I'm not worth it.” In the fact – interpretation – meaning distinction, “Apparently I'm not worth it” is the…

options.text: fact
interpretation
meaning
consequence

te.explanation: Fact = “She looked away.” Interpretation = “She doesn't find me interesting.” Meaning = “Apparently I'm not worth it” (what it says about the client). Separating these lets you ask, e.g., “What else could explain that she looked away?”→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: A psychologist has just read three articles about autism in women. The next day, with a shy young woman, autism is the first explanation that comes to mind and she hardly considers social anxiety. Which cognitive error is this?

options.text: Anchoring bias
The availability heuristic
Solution reflex
Gradual disclosure

te.explanation: Availability heuristic = more readily considering explanations that easily come to mind (here: because she just read about it). Anchoring = sticking to a first impression after new information; solution reflex = advice too early; gradual disclosure isn't an error at all but a client phenomenon.→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: According to Lecture 4, what happens after the diagnostic cycle ends with the advice / feedback session?

options.text: The referral phase starts again immediately.
The psychologist adds a DSM classification.
The therapy (treatment) cycle then starts.
The client is discharged from care.

te.explanation: The class question “When does this cycle end? And then?” → it ends with the advice (Adv); then the therapy cycle starts. Classification happened earlier (problem analysis).→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: Which is NOT one of the legal and professional checks at referral mentioned in Lecture 4?

options.text: Consent: who may commission the assessment and who must consent?
Limits of competence: does the question fit your expertise and institution?
Need for assessment: is further additional assessment proportionate to the problem?
Treatment choice: which therapy has the best evidence for this problem?

te.explanation: The five checks are consent, privacy/GDPR, minors, limits of competence and need for (proportionality of) assessment. Treatment choice belongs to the indication analysis, much later in the cycle.→ re-read Lecture 4

te.question: During the problem analysis for Sem (10), the psychologist (1) interviews his grandmother, who raised him until he was 6, and (2) reads earlier psychological reports and his medication records. Which two methods are these?

options.text: Case history and systematic observation
Collateral history and file review
Diagnostic interview and broad screening
Self-monitoring and hetero-observation at home

te.explanation: Methods used during the problem analysis: case history/diagnostic interview · collateral history (interview with partner, parents or other significant others) · observation · questionnaires/screening (SCL-90, SDQ) · file review/document analysis (previous reports, school reports, work evaluations, medication records).→ re-read Lecture 7

te.question: A 15-year-old has been skipping school, sleeping badly and avoiding friends for eight months, since he was bullied online; his grades have dropped. Which combination of Rutter's criteria points most strongly to greater severity?

options.text: Persistent, interferes with other areas, linked to stress
Age-appropriate, short-lived, isolated, and not interfering with school
Situation-specific, recent, infrequent, and unrelated to any stress
Fits the sociocultural background, infrequent, and not persistent

te.explanation: Eight months = persistent; school, friends and grades = interferes with other areas; online bullying = psychosocial stress; several problems together = not isolated. The other options describe signals of lower severity.→ re-read Lecture 7

te.question: Why does Lecture 7 stress mapping protective factors during the problem analysis?

options.text: Because protective factors directly determine the DSM classification and the final diagnostic label.
Because protective factors make the explanatory analysis unnecessary later in the diagnostic cycle.
Because health insurers and legal regulations require them in the written psychological report.
Because they inform severity, give perspective, and offer a starting point for treatment.

te.explanation: Weighing adaptive and maladaptive behaviour: protective factors (1) inform severity, (2) put problems into perspective, (3) give a starting point for treatment — build on the person's strengths.→ re-read Lecture 7

te.question: In the problem analysis the psychologist completes the (often incomplete) complaint analysis with missing information. Which method is typically used in this phase, according to the lecture?

options.text: (Semi-)structured interviews
Projective tests
Brain scans
Therapy evaluation questionnaires

te.explanation: General problem inventory: the complaint analysis is based on the client's experience and is often incomplete → complete it. “This is often the phase of the diagnostic cycle where (semi-)structured interviews are conducted.” Other methods: collateral history, observation, questionnaires (SCL-90, SDQ), file review.→ re-read Lecture 7

te.question: I. One of Rutter's criteria asks whether the problem behaviour also interferes with other areas, such as family, social functioning and development.II. Rutter's criteria are mainly used to decide which explanatory condition maintains a problem.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

te.explanation: I is correct (the “interferes with other areas” criterion). II is wrong: Rutter's criteria (1975) belong to the assessment of severity in the problem analysis; conditions that maintain a problem are the subject of the explanatory analysis.→ re-read Lecture 7

te.question: A psychologist writes: “Research shows that children of divorced parents more often develop attention problems; therefore the divorce caused Mila's attention problems.” Which requirement for a causal claim is most clearly missing?

options.text: Temporal order and ruling out alternative explanations for this child
A correlation between the two variables in the group data
The presence of a problem in the child at present
A clearly defined level of analysis for describing the problem

te.explanation: A correlation at group level is there (B). For causality you also need: the cause comes before the effect, a plausible mechanism backed by (preferably longitudinal/experimental) research, and alternative explanations reasonably ruled out (confounders, common cause, reverse causality) — for this client.→ re-read Lecture 8

te.question: What is the main danger of explaining a problem at the disorder level (e.g. “…because of the depressive disorder”)?

options.text: It is too biological and ignores the person's psychological context.
It risks a tautology: the label just repeats the problem.
It is not allowed by the DSM or the ICD.
It can only be used in HiTOP and RDoC research

te.explanation: The slide lists the disorder level (DSM/ICD) with a “but…”: a disorder is not a condition. “Sad because depressed” is a tautology, and people with the same disorder differ widely. Alternatives: the spectrum level (HiTOP) or individual symptoms (network), plus real conditions such as avoidance or poor sleep.→ re-read Lecture 8

te.question: Which of the following is an example of reverse causality?

options.text: Social exclusion leads to both being bullied and to developing depression later on.
Stress leads to depression, but mostly in people who ruminate quite a lot.
Poor sleep is assumed to cause low mood, but the reverse may hold.
Early divorce leads to problematic personality development, which then leads to learning delay.

te.explanation: Reverse causality: the supposed effect is (also) the cause — the slide's example is depression ↔ sleep problems. A = common cause; B = moderation; D = a chain (mediation) as in the lecture's schematic example.→ re-read Lecture 8

te.question: Hypothesis: “Emma's concentration problems are partly caused by poor sleep.” Criterion set in advance: “average sleep < 6 hours on at least 10 of 14 nights” in a sleep diary. The diary shows 7–8 hours of sleep on 13 of 14 nights. What happens to the hypothesis?

options.text: Accept the hypothesis
Retain the hypothesis
Reject the hypothesis
Reformulate the hypothesis

te.explanation: The criterion is clearly not met → reject. Retain = the evidence is inconclusive, so you keep the hypothesis open and assess further. This is why you set a testing criterion before testing: “without a clear test criterion, testing is of little use.”→ re-read Lecture 8

te.question: How should a rejected hypothesis be handled in the integrative formulation?

options.text: Leave it out: only accepted hypotheses answer the help question.
Mention it only if the client asks about it directly.
Report it together with the results that ruled it out.
Keep reformulating it until it can eventually be accepted again.

te.explanation: The integrative formulation integrates accepted, retained and rejected hypotheses (+ options for further assessment). The slide gives exactly this kind of sentence for a rejected hypothesis. Ruling things out is informative for the client and the referrer.→ re-read Lecture 8

te.question: A student searches the literature for: “Is worrying a risk factor for both depression and anxiety?” Which search direction and which type of condition is this?

options.text: From problem to condition; a specific condition
From condition to problem; a transdiagnostic condition
From problem to condition; a transdiagnostic condition
From condition to problem; a specific condition

te.explanation: It starts from a possible explanatory condition (worrying) and asks which problems it leads to → from condition to problem (the slide's own example). A condition linked to several problems is transdiagnostic (like neuroticism, rumination/worry, RDoC domains); a specific condition links to one problem (e.g. OCD and metacognitive confidence).→ re-read Lecture 8

epc1.question: A researcher measures how many seconds participants keep their hand in ice water, and calls this “pain tolerance”. This is an example of _____.

options.text: an operational definition
analytical introspection
a cognitive function
apparent motion

epc1.explanation: An operational definition describes an abstract property (pain tolerance) as a concrete measurable condition (seconds). Introspection is self-observation of conscious content; a cognitive function is a building block like memory; apparent motion is a Gestalt illusion.

epc1.question: Which pair of school and central claim is NOT correct?

options.text: Structuralism — consciousness can be broken down into its basic elements
Functionalism — mental processes serve a useful purpose for human adaptation
Gestalt psychology — the whole exceeds the sum of its parts
Behaviourism — introspection is the best way to study the mind

epc1.explanation: Behaviourism rejects introspection as too vague and subjective and studies overt behaviour instead. The other three pairs are correct.

epc1.question: Donders measured a simple RT of 198 ms, a go/no-go RT of 269 ms and a choice RT of 299 ms. How long does decision making alone take?

options.text: 71 ms
101 ms
30 ms
269 ms

epc1.explanation: Decision alone = choice − go/no-go = 299 − 269 = 30 ms. 71 ms (269 − 198) is discrimination; 101 ms (299 − 198) is discrimination plus decision.

epc1.question: A patient can describe a pair of glasses, a nose and a mouth, but cannot tell whose face it is; recognising objects is no problem. This is _____.

options.text: visual agnosia
neglect
prosopagnosia
aphasia

epc1.explanation: Faces impaired, objects intact = prosopagnosia. Visual agnosia is the opposite pattern (objects impaired); neglect is ignoring one side of space; aphasia concerns speech.

epc1.question: Which philosopher belongs to a different group than the other three?

options.text: John Locke
George Berkeley
David Hume
Gottfried Leibniz

epc1.explanation: Locke, Berkeley and Hume are British empiricists (knowledge is acquired). Leibniz is a continental rationalist (knowledge is innate — nativism).

epc1.question: A teacher stops giving a hated weekly test because the class works quietly. The quiet working increases. This is _____.

options.text: positive reinforcement
negative reinforcement
positive punishment
negative punishment

epc1.explanation: Something unpleasant (the test) is removed = negative, and the behaviour increases = reinforcement → negative reinforcement. Remember: positive/negative = added/removed, not nice/nasty.

epc1.question:
Statement I: According to Descartes' dualism, body and mind are separate entities that interact via the pineal gland.
Statement II: Nativism claims that knowledge is acquired through experience.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

epc1.explanation: I is correct. II is wrong: nativism says knowledge is innate; acquiring knowledge through experience is empiricism.

epc1.question: A row of lamps switches on one after another and you see one moving light. Gestalt psychologists used this to argue that _____.

options.text: sensation and perception are really the same thing
perception constructs experience rather than reflecting the sensation
consciousness consists of about 44 000 elemental qualities
psychology should study observable behaviour using objective measurement

epc1.explanation: This is apparent motion (the phi phenomenon): the sensations are separate flashes, but perception builds movement out of them. The 44 000 elemental qualities belong to Titchener (structuralism).

epc1.question: Which statement about the JND is correct?

options.text: It is the largest difference that still goes unnoticed
It is the minimum difference detected 50% of the time
It is the minimum difference detected 25% of the time
It was introduced by Donders in his reaction-time studies

epc1.explanation: The JND (Fechner, inspired by Weber) = the minimum difference detectable 50% of the time. Donders is mental chronometry.

epc1.question: Which description fits cognitive neuroscience best?

options.text: Studying patients with local brain damage to infer normal function
Breaking consciousness into basic sensations and feelings through introspection
Understanding the biological foundations of cognition by tracking brain activity
Predicting and controlling overt behaviour for the benefit of society

epc1.explanation: That is the definition on the slide. Option A describes cognitive neuropsychology, B is structuralism and D is behaviourism.

epc2.question: A researcher claims “children who eat breakfast get better grades, so breakfast improves school performance”. The weakest point of this claim is _____.

options.text: that the sample was probably far too small
that grades are a qualitative rather than numerical measure
that breakfast cannot be properly operationalised in studies
a third variable, e.g. family income, causing both

epc2.explanation: A correlation is never evidence for causation: a third variable (income, home routine, sleep) may cause both. Sample size is a different issue; grades are quantitative; breakfast is easy to operationalise.

epc2.question:
Statement I: According to Popper, more supporting observations make a theory more true.
Statement II: Hume pointed out that unencountered exceptions may always arise.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

epc2.explanation: Popper said the opposite: theories can only be falsified, never proven true by more cases. Statement II is exactly Hume's point.

epc2.question: Participants in a study called “Effects of sleep loss on mood” report feeling miserable mainly because they guess what the researcher expects. This is _____.

options.text: observer bias
participant reactivity
demand characteristics
Type II error

epc2.explanation: Demand characteristics: participants act according to what they believe is 'demanded' of them. Observer bias sits with the researcher; reactivity is the more general fact that being observed changes behaviour; a Type II error is a missed effect.

epc2.question: Which design is between-subjects?

options.text: Everyone does the task once before and once after drinking coffee
Half the participants work in quiet, the other half in noise
Every participant rates all 40 pictures presented in a random order
Each participant is tested at 9 AM, 1 PM and 5 PM

epc2.explanation: Different participants receive different levels of the manipulation = between-subjects. The other three give every level to every participant = within-subjects.

epc2.question: A test always gives the same score for the same person, but it does not measure what it claims to measure. The test is _____.

options.text: valid but not reliable
reliable but not valid
neither valid nor reliable
both valid and reliable

epc2.explanation: Consistent = reliable; wrong target = not valid. That is the second target picture: all shots together, but far from the bullseye.

epc2.question: Which is the best example of a Type I error?

options.text: Concluding the drug is useless while it actually works
Measuring participants' mood with an unreliable, inconsistent self-report questionnaire
Sampling mostly WEIRD participants, which limits generalisation to others
Concluding the drug works while it really does nothing

epc2.explanation: A Type I error is a false alarm: an observed effect that is not real. Option A is a Type II error; B is reliability; C is an external-validity problem.

epc2.question: Why is randomization important in an experiment?

options.text: It increases the sample size of the experiment
It guarantees a significant p-value in the results
It keeps group assignment independent of any third variable
It turns qualitative data into quantitative data automatically

epc2.explanation: Randomization means every member of the population of interest has an equal chance of being selected and assignment is not driven by a third variable — that is what lets you attribute differences to your manipulation.

epc2.question: “Most Dutch people are 182.9 cm tall on average.” Which measure is this?

options.text: Mean
Median
Mode
Range

epc2.explanation: The arithmetic average = the mean. The mode is the most frequent value, the median splits the ordered data in half, the range is the distance between lowest and highest.

epc2.question: Which statement about WEIRD samples is correct?

options.text: They are 16% of humanity but heavily overrepresented
They are the most reliable participants for research
They threaten internal validity rather than external validity
They are deliberately used to guarantee random assignment

epc2.explanation: WEIRD = Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic — roughly 16% of the human race, yet heavily overrepresented. That limits external validity (generalisability).

epc2.question: An experiment is set up so that the conclusion “X caused Y” is actually justified, but only for this specific student sample in this lab. This experiment has _____.

options.text: high internal validity and limited external validity
high external validity and low internal validity
low internal and low external validity
neither — this is about reliability

epc2.explanation: Internal validity = the causal inference inside the study is accurate. External validity = whether it generalises to other samples and settings, which is exactly what is limited here.

epc3.question: A researcher wants to know exactly when, to the millisecond, the brain responds to a sound. Which method fits best?

options.text: fMRI
PET
CT
EEG

epc3.explanation: EEG has the highest temporal resolution of the scalp methods (millisecond precision). fMRI and PET are slow (blood flow); CT shows structure, not activity.

epc3.question: A patient can understand everything you say but produces almost no speech. The damage is most likely in _____.

options.text: left temporal lobe (Wernicke's area)
left frontal lobe (Broca's area)
the occipital lobe (visual cortex)
the corpus callosum (connecting fibres)

epc3.explanation: Production impaired + comprehension intact = Broca (left frontal). Wernicke's damage gives the opposite pattern.

epc3.question: Which statement about grey and white matter is correct?

options.text: Grey matter is made of cell bodies, white matter of axons
Grey matter consists of axons, white matter of cell bodies
Both consist of cell bodies, but white matter is thicker
White matter is found only in the corpus callosum itself

epc3.explanation: Grey = cell bodies, white = the connections (axons). The corpus callosum is made of white matter, but white matter is everywhere.

epc3.question: A split-brain patient is shown a picture of a clock in the left visual field. Which outcome is expected?

options.text: He names the clock correctly but cannot draw it afterwards
He draws it left-handed but cannot say what it was
He can neither draw the clock nor name it afterwards
He names it correctly and draws it with the right hand

epc3.explanation: Left visual field → right hemisphere → controls the left hand (drawing works) but has no speech, so naming fails.

epc3.question: Which method is used to change brain activity rather than measure it?

options.text: MEG
PET
Single-cell recording
TMS

epc3.explanation: TMS (and tDCS) stimulate or inhibit nerve cells — TMS is used therapeutically for depression. The others only measure.

epc3.question: Which combination of resolutions belongs to fMRI?

options.text: High spatial, high temporal
Low spatial, high temporal
High spatial, low temporal
Low spatial, low temporal

epc3.explanation: fMRI follows blood flow, which is slow → low temporal resolution, but it localises well → high spatial resolution. High/high is MEG (and single-cell); low spatial + high temporal is EEG.

epc3.question: Phineas Gage's accident is mainly used to show that _____.

options.text: the occipital lobe is responsible for vision
the corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres
the frontal lobe underlies executive functioning and personality
language production depends on the temporal lobe

epc3.explanation: His personality and self-control changed dramatically after frontal damage; the Stroop task is the classic measure of that kind of executive control.

epc3.question: Why does the cortex have gyri and sulci?

options.text: To neatly separate grey from white matter
To add surface area and processing power
To protect the corpus callosum from damage
To speed up action potentials along axons

epc3.explanation: Folding packs much more cortical surface into the skull, which means more capacity for processing information.

epc3.question:
Statement I: MRI and fMRI use the same kind of machine but answer different questions.
Statement II: EEG has excellent spatial resolution because each electrode records the cortex directly beneath it.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

epc3.explanation: I is correct: MRI = structure, fMRI = activity through blood flow. II is wrong: EEG has poor spatial resolution — activity at one electrode need not come from directly underneath.

epc3.question: Which technique measures the activity of a single neuron with very precise localisation?

options.text: Single-cell recording
MEG
EEG
PET

epc3.explanation: An electrode placed at the cell measures its action potentials — high temporal resolution and very precise localisation, but extremely invasive.

epc4.question: A patient can point to and correctly grasp a cup — sensation is fine — but cannot say what the object is or that it is a cup at all. This dissociation is a textbook illustration of the difference between _____.

options.text: the rods and cones
trichromatic and opponent-process theory
sensation and perceptual recognition
frequency theory and place theory

epc4.explanation: Sensation is awareness from stimulating a sense organ; perception is organizing, identifying and interpreting that sensation into a mental representation. In (apperceptive) visual form agnosia, sensation is intact but the perceptual step of recognizing the object fails.

epc4.question: A standard weight of 200 grams has a Weber fraction of .05 for judgments of heaviness. How heavy must a comparison weight be for it to be judged heavier on 50% of trials?

options.text: 210 grams
205 grams
220 grams
240 grams

epc4.explanation: Weber's law: the JND is a constant proportion (the Weber fraction) of the standard. JND = .05 × 200 g = 10 g, so the comparison must be 200 + 10 = 210 g.

epc4.question: In a signal detection experiment, a participant answers 'yes, I heard a tone' on a trial where, in fact, no tone was presented. This response type is called a _____.

options.text: hit
miss
correct rejection
false alarm

epc4.explanation: Hit = yes + stimulus present; miss = no + stimulus present; correct rejection = no + no stimulus; false alarm = yes + no stimulus, as here. A liberal response criterion produces more hits and more false alarms.

epc4.question: Why are both the trichromatic theory and the opponent-process theory needed to explain color vision?

options.text: Trichromatic theory explains afterimages and perceived hue; opponent-process theory explains how cones detect wavelengths at receptors
Trichromatic theory explains wavelength detection by three cone types; opponent-process theory explains ganglion-cell wiring and afterimages
Opponent-process theory has replaced trichromatic theory, which turned out to be wrong for human color vision
Trichromatic theory applies to rods, and opponent-process theory applies to cones in the retina periphery

epc4.explanation: The two theories work at different levels: trichromatic theory (Young-Helmholtz) at the receptor level (S/M/L cones), opponent-process theory (Hering) at the ganglion/neural level — which is also how it explains negative color afterimages.

epc4.question: Frequency theory says pitch is coded by the firing rate of auditory neurons. This works for low tones, but runs into a problem for high tones because _____.

options.text: a single neuron cannot fire faster than about 1,000 times per second
high tones are blocked by the middle ear before reaching the cochlea
high tones stimulate only the vestibular system rather than the cochlea
the oval window does not vibrate at frequencies above a certain level

epc4.explanation: A neuron's maximal firing rate is ≈1,000 Hz, but humans hear tones far above that — so place theory (Békésy) is needed: different frequencies peak at different places on the basilar membrane.

epc4.question: Vibration of the eardrum passes through the three ossicles of the middle ear. What is the correct order, from the eardrum to the oval window?

options.text: stirrup → anvil → hammer
anvil → hammer → stirrup
hammer → anvil → stirrup
hammer → stirrup → anvil

epc4.explanation: The hammer (malleus) touches the eardrum, the anvil (incus) sits in the middle, and the stirrup (stapes) presses on the oval window. These are the three smallest bones in the human body.

epc4.question: Which structure is the FIRST point in the auditory pathway that receives input from both ears?

options.text: cochlear nucleus
inferior colliculus
medial geniculate body
superior olivary complex

epc4.explanation: Cochlea → cochlear nucleus (mostly crosses to the contralateral side) → superior olivary complex (first binaural convergence) → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex (A1).

epc4.question: Why is ITD (interaural time difference) a better localization cue than ILD for LOW-frequency sounds?

options.text: Low-frequency sounds cannot bend around the head, creating a large acoustic shadow between the ears
Low-frequency sounds bend around the head, so loudness barely differs while timing still helps localization
ILD cannot be measured for low-frequency sounds because the ears are too close together
Low-frequency sounds travel faster through air than high-frequency sounds and arrive sooner at both ears

epc4.explanation: Low frequencies bend around the head, so loudness (ILD) barely differs between ears — leaving timing (ITD) as the informative cue. High frequencies cannot bend around the head (acoustic shadow), which is why ILD works best for them. All sound travels at the same speed through air, regardless of frequency.

epc4.question: A listener cannot tell whether a sound came from straight ahead or from directly behind. The best explanation is _____.

options.text: damage to the superior olive in the auditory brainstem
the sound was just below the absolute hearing threshold
ITD and ILD are both ≈0: the cone of confusion
the sound had no distinct timbre or pitch quality

epc4.explanation: For sounds on the midline, front and back locations produce the same (≈0) interaural time and level differences, so many possible locations are indistinguishable from binaural cues alone — the cone of confusion. Pinna shape, echoes, head movement and vision resolve most of the ambiguity in practice.

epc4.question: A person sees a speaker's mouth forming /ga/ while the soundtrack actually plays /ba/. Most viewers report hearing /da/. This is called the _____, and shows that _____.

options.text: McGurk effect; visual and auditory input fuse into a new percept
ventriloquist effect; the sound's perceived location shifts toward the seen mouth
cone of confusion; ITD and ILD cues cannot be resolved here
gate-control effect; touch input can suppress an incoming auditory sound signal

epc4.explanation: This is the McGurk effect: mismatched visual (/ga/) and auditory (/ba/) speech information fuse into a new percept (/da/) — direct evidence for multisensory integration in speech perception. The ventriloquist effect instead relocates where a sound seems to come from, not what it sounds like.

epc4.question: Why does rubbing a painful area often make it feel less painful, according to gate-control theory?

options.text: Rubbing activates A-delta fibers, which carry touch signals rather than pain
Rubbing numbs the C fibers directly at the site of injury
Rubbing releases endorphins in the periaqueductal grey, blocking the pain signal
Rubbing activates A-beta touch fibers, which can close the spinal 'gate'

epc4.explanation: A-beta fibers, activated by light touch and pressure, can close the gate in the spinal dorsal horn, reducing how much pain signal reaches the brain. (A-delta fibers actually carry sharp pain, not touch; endorphins/PAG describe a different, brain-driven route to pain relief, triggered by stress rather than by rubbing.)

epc4.question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Semicircular canals in the inner ear detect head rotation in three axes, while otoliths detect linear acceleration and gravity's pull on the head.
The five basic tastes — sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami — are all equally uncontroversial; umami's status as a basic taste is settled.
Information from the olfactory epithelium reaches the olfactory bulb on the same side of the head; crossing to the other hemisphere happens only downstream.
About half of a person's taste receptors are gone by around age 20, which may partly explain why children seem to be 'fussy eaters'.

epc4.explanation: Umami was only recognized as a distinct taste in 1908, and the slides explicitly note that its existence as a separate basic taste is still debated — so statement B is false. The other three statements are directly from the material.

epc4.question: A 45-year-old suddenly has to hold their phone at arm's length to read it, while their distance vision is still fine. Which problem is this, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Myopia; a concave (–) lens corrects it
Astigmatism; a cylinder lens corrects it
Presbyopia; a convex (+) lens corrects it
Cataract; a concave (–) lens corrects it

epc4.explanation: Presbyopia is age-related farsightedness (from ~40 years): the lens hardens and loses its elasticity, so it can no longer focus on close objects. Corrected with reading glasses (+ powered convex lens). Myopia blurs distant objects; astigmatism blurs all distances; cataract is a cloudy lens.

epc4.question: In someone's eye, light comes into focus behind the retina because the eyeball is too short. Which description fits?

options.text: Hyperopia: close objects are blurred; convex lens
Myopia: close objects are blurred; concave lens
Hyperopia: distant objects are blurred; concave lens
Myopia: distant objects are blurred; convex lens

epc4.explanation: Eye too short → focal plane behind the retina = hyperopia (farsighted): close objects can't be focused; corrected with a convex (+) lens. The opposite is myopia: eye too long, focal plane in front of the retina, distant objects blurred, concave (–) lens.

epc4.question: A patient still sees sharply in the centre of what they look at, but over the years slowly loses vision at the edges of the visual field. Which condition fits best?

options.text: Macular degeneration, damage to the fovea
Cataract, clouding of the lens
Astigmatism, irregular curvature of the cornea
Glaucoma, nerve cells failing from pressure

epc4.explanation: Glaucoma = worsening/loss of peripheral vision because nerve cells fail due to increased eye pressure. Macular degeneration is the opposite: the fovea degenerates, so the centre becomes black and distorted. Cataract clouds the whole image; astigmatism blurs at all distances.

epc5.question: Sperling flashed a grid of 12 letters for 50 ms and then played a tone telling participants which row to report. Almost the whole row was recalled. What does this show?

options.text: Iconic memory can hold about 4–5 letters at a time
The tone improved the encoding of the cued row of letters
Echoic memory lasts several seconds longer than iconic memory does
All letters were briefly stored but fade before they are reported

epc5.explanation: Because the tone came after the display, participants could not know which row to prepare — so being able to report any cued row means all letters were in iconic memory. 4–5 is what survives long enough for whole report; delaying the tone shows the decay (~150 ms).

epc5.question: A student learns French, then Spanish, and afterwards struggles with the French exam. This is _____.

options.text: proactive interference
retroactive interference
blocking
transience

epc5.explanation: The new material (Spanish) works backwards on the older memory (French) = retroactive. Proactive would be French disturbing the later Spanish.

epc5.question: Which component of working memory would be most disturbed by listening to music with lyrics while studying text?

options.text: The visuospatial sketchpad
The episodic buffer
The phonological loop
The central executive only

epc5.explanation: Lyrics are verbal, so they compete for the phonological loop — the classic dual-task interference result (Salamé & Baddeley, 1989). Doodling, being visual, would hit the sketchpad instead.

epc5.question: Patient H.M. could learn mirror writing but never remembered practising it. Which distinction does this illustrate?

options.text: Implicit memory spared, explicit memory impaired
Semantic versus episodic long-term memory
Retrograde versus transient global amnesia
Recall versus recognition memory tests

epc5.explanation: Skills are implicit/procedural memory, which survives; the conscious record of the practice sessions is explicit and does not form. This is the standard amnesia pattern.

epc5.question: Craik and Tulving had people judge words for capital letters, rhyme, or meaning. Which order of later recall is correct?

options.text: visual < phonemic < semantic
semantic < phonemic < visual
phonemic < visual < semantic
all three were equal

epc5.explanation: Deeper processing = better memory: judging meaning beats judging sound, which beats judging appearance. This is the levels-of-processing effect.

epc5.question: A witness is asked how fast the cars went when they “crashed into” each other rather than “bumped into” each other. She gives a higher speed and also remembers broken glass that was never there. This demonstrates _____.

options.text: transience
proactive interference
state-dependent retrieval
suggestibility

epc5.explanation: Loftus & Palmer (1974): the wording of the question is incorporated into the memory — the seventh-sin category suggestibility, which is why eye-witness interviews must be worded neutrally.

epc5.question: Which statement about LTP is correct?

options.text: It happens mainly in the cerebellum and brainstem
It weakens synapses that are used too often
Glutamate must bind NMDA receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
It only occurs during deep, slow-wave sleep phases

epc5.explanation: LTP is the persistent strengthening of synapses, shown most convincingly in the hippocampus; it starts when glutamate from the sending neuron binds NMDA receptors on the receiving neuron — which only works if that neuron is already excited.

epc5.question: Ribot's law says that in retrograde amnesia _____.

options.text: no new memories can be formed after the injury
the oldest childhood memories are lost before recent ones
the most recent memories are lost first, old ones spared
implicit memory is usually lost long before explicit memory

epc5.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is usually temporally graded: recent memories go first. “No new memories” describes anterograde amnesia.

epc5.question:
Statement I: The episodic buffer is a part of working memory.
Statement II: Episodic memory is a type of implicit memory.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

epc5.explanation: I is correct (Baddeley's fourth component). II is wrong: episodic memory is explicit (conscious) long-term memory — the slides warn not to confuse it with the episodic buffer.

epc5.question: A patient invents detailed memories that never happened, cannot form new memories, and has a history of alcoholism. This fits _____.

options.text: dissociative fugue
Korsakoff syndrome
transient global amnesia
childhood amnesia

epc5.explanation: Korsakoff: chronic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, confabulations, anterograde and retrograde amnesia, executive dysfunction — and it is irreversible. TGA resolves quickly; dissociative amnesia is functional, without brain pathology.

epc6.question: Your neighbour's dog barking didn't bother you at first, but after weeks of daily barking you now get irritated within seconds of it starting — and you've also become jumpier at loud kitchen noises you never minded before. What is happening?

options.text: Sensitization — an increased response that can spread to other stimuli
Habituation — the response has become specific to that one stimulus
Classical conditioning — the dog has become a CS for irritation
Negative reinforcement — the barking is being removed by your irritation

epc6.explanation: The response has increased, not decreased, so this is not habituation. And it has spread to an unrelated stimulus (kitchen noises) — exactly the pattern the slides describe for sensitization, which (unlike habituation) is not stimulus-specific. No pairing of two stimuli or consequence-based learning is described, so classical/operant conditioning don't fit.

epc6.question: You put on strong perfume in the morning and after ten minutes you can no longer smell it on yourself, even though a friend who just walked in notices it immediately. What best explains why you stopped smelling it?

options.text: Habituation — a behavioural change in how you respond to it
Sensory adaptation — your smell receptor cells have physically adapted
Extinction — the perfume (CS) is no longer paired with anything
Sensitization — repeated exposure to the perfume has increased your sensitivity

epc6.explanation: Because a friend with a fresh nose still smells it, the perfume is still physically present — it is your receptor cells that have adapted, which is sensory adaptation, a physiological effect. Habituation would be a behavioural change; there is no CS/US pairing here, and sensitivity has decreased, not increased.

epc6.question: Watson made a loud, frightening noise every time he showed baby 'Little Albert' a white rat. After several pairings, Albert began to cry as soon as the rat appeared, even without the noise. In this study, the white rat is the ___.

options.text: unconditioned stimulus (US)
unconditioned response (UR)
conditioned stimulus (CS)
conditioned response (CR)

epc6.explanation: The rat started out neutral and only came to trigger crying after being paired with the noise — that makes it the CS. The loud noise is the US (it caused fear without any learning), the original fear/crying to the noise is the UR, and Albert's crying at the rat after conditioning is the CR.

epc6.question: A dog has learned to salivate to a bell that predicts food. The experimenter then rings the bell many times with no food, and salivation gradually stops. A week later, with no further training, a single ring of the bell makes the dog salivate again, if only briefly. The two processes described here are, in order, ___.

options.text: generalization, then discrimination
acquisition, then blocking
sensitization, then habituation
extinction, then spontaneous recovery

epc6.explanation: Presenting the CS (bell) without the US (food) until the CR fades is extinction; the CR briefly reappearing after a rest period, without any relearning, is spontaneous recovery. Generalization/discrimination concern similar stimuli, not the passage of time, and blocking concerns a second, new CS.

epc6.question: A child becomes afraid of the sound of a dentist's drill after it was repeatedly paired with pain. Later, simply walking into the dentist's waiting room — which the child has often seen right before hearing the drill, but which was never itself paired with pain — is now enough to make the child cry. This is best explained by ___.

options.text: biological preparedness
second-order conditioning
Kamin's blocking
stimulus generalization

epc6.explanation: The waiting room (a new, neutral stimulus) became frightening only because it was paired with the already-conditioned drill sound, not with pain itself — the definition of second-order conditioning. It is not preparedness (no special evolutionary link to fear here), not blocking (no earlier CS is preventing new learning), and not generalization (the waiting room is not similar in appearance to the drill).

epc6.question: After eating shellfish for the first time, a man develops a stomach flu six hours later that has nothing to do with the food. He nonetheless develops a strong, lasting aversion to shellfish, even though the illness came far too long after eating for ordinary classical conditioning (which usually needs the CS and US close together in time) to explain it. This is best explained by ___.

options.text: second-order conditioning to the shellfish
Thorndike's law of effect
biological preparedness for taste-illness links
discrimination training between different foods

epc6.explanation: Taste aversion shows that contiguity is not always necessary: animals (and people) are biologically prepared to link a taste to later illness even across a long delay, exactly as in Garcia and Koelling's rats. The law of effect is about operant behaviour and consequences, not classical conditioning; there is no second stimulus becoming linked to an established CS, and no discrimination task is involved.

epc6.question: Rats first learn that a tone predicts a shock. Once that association is strong, a light is added alongside the tone before further shocks. Afterwards, the rats fear the tone but show no fear of the light on its own. This outcome — an established CS preventing a new CS from being learned — is called ___.

options.text: Kamin's blocking
second-order conditioning
spontaneous recovery
overjustification effect

epc6.explanation: This is Kamin's classic blocking result: because the tone already fully predicted the shock, the light added no new information and was never learned as a CS. It is not second-order conditioning (the light was paired with the US directly, not with the tone as a stand-in US), not spontaneous recovery (no extinction or rest period here), and not the overjustification effect (that concerns rewards undermining intrinsic motivation).

epc6.question: A café gives you a free coffee every time you have bought exactly nine, always on the ninth purchase. A rewards app instead gives you a small bonus at unpredictable moments, averaging one bonus per twenty logins. Which schedule keeps you responding the most steadily, without any pause right after a reward?

options.text: fixed interval (the café)
fixed ratio (the café)
variable interval (the app)
variable ratio (the app)

epc6.explanation: The café is a fixed ratio schedule (reward after a fixed number of responses), which produces a high rate but with a post-reinforcement pause. The app is a variable ratio schedule (reward after an unpredictable number of responses), which produces a high, steady rate with no pauses — and is the schedule most resistant to extinction. Neither is based on elapsed time, so the interval options don't apply.

epc6.question: A teenager loses his phone (something he enjoys having) for a week after breaking curfew, and afterwards he stops breaking curfew. In the reinforcement/punishment scheme, this is ___.

options.text: positive reinforcement
negative reinforcement
negative punishment
positive punishment

epc6.explanation: A pleasant stimulus (the phone) is removed (= negative) and the behaviour decreases (= punishment), so this is negative punishment. It is not reinforcement of any kind because the target behaviour goes down, not up, and it is not positive punishment because nothing unpleasant was added.

epc6.question: Rats explore a maze for ten days with no reward at the goal box and show only slow improvement. From day eleven onward, food is placed at the goal, and within a day or two their performance improves dramatically, nearly matching rats that had been rewarded from day one. This supports the idea that ___.

options.text: reinforcement must be given continuously to have any effect on behaviour
the rats needed operant shaping before they could learn the maze
the rats were showing spontaneous recovery of a previously extinguished response
the rats had already learned the maze layout — latent learning

epc6.explanation: The sudden jump in performance as soon as reward is introduced shows the rats had already learned the maze's layout during the unrewarded days — Tolman's latent learning: learning that does not show up in behaviour until it becomes useful to show it. There was no earlier CR to spontaneously recover, no shaping procedure was used, and behaviour clearly was not shaped only by continuous reinforcement.

epc7.question: A child hears the word "dogs". How many morphemes does it contain, and why?

options.text: 1 — it is a single word
2 — "dog" and the plural "-s"
4 — one for each phoneme
3 — "d", "og" and "s"

epc7.explanation: "dogs" contains two morphemes: the free morpheme "dog" and the bound morpheme plural "-s". Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units — phonemes (the sounds /d/,/ɒ/,/g/,/z/) carry no meaning by themselves.

epc7.question: An ambiguous sound halfway between "g" and "k" is heard as "g" when followed by "-ift" but as "k" when followed by "-iss". This is called the _____.

options.text: Ganong effect
Sapir-Whorf effect
wug effect
poverty-of-stimulus effect

epc7.explanation: This is the Ganong effect (Ganong, 1980): the mental lexicon pulls an ambiguous sound towards whichever real word it completes ("gift" and "kiss" are words; "kift" and "giss" are not). The Sapir–Whorf idea is about language shaping thought, not speech perception.

epc7.question: Which statement about categorical perception of speech sounds is correct?

options.text: Equal physical steps along a continuum are always perceived as equally different
It only appears in adults after they have learned to read
Two sounds are easier to tell apart when identified as different categories
It disappears completely again within the first few weeks of life

epc7.explanation: Discrimination is easier across a category boundary — we seem to store the category (/ba/ or /da/), not the fine acoustic detail. The identification curve is S-shaped, not linear, so option A is wrong; categorical perception is present from under 8 weeks of age and narrows with experience rather than vanishing (option D).

epc7.question: A patient speaks fluently and grammatically, but the content is meaningless, and she cannot understand spoken language at all. This best fits _____.

options.text: Broca's aphasia
genetic dysphasia
developmental dyslexia
Wernicke's aphasia

epc7.explanation: Fluent but meaningless speech plus a comprehension deficit is the signature of Wernicke's aphasia. Broca's aphasia is the opposite pattern: non-fluent, telegram-style, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension of simple language.

epc7.question: According to Chomsky, which pair correctly matches the terms to their meaning?

options.text: Deep structure = universal conceptual meaning; surface structure = actual word sequence
Deep structure = actual word order; surface structure = universal conceptual meaning
Deep and surface structure both refer to word order in different languages
Transformational rules turn surface structure into deep structure in the speaker's brain

epc7.explanation: The deep structure is the language-independent conceptual meaning; the surface structure is the specific word sequence used to express it. Transformational rules generate a surface structure that fits the deep structure — not the reverse.

epc7.question: Which finding is used as evidence AGAINST strict linguistic determinism (Whorf), and FOR the weaker linguistic relativity view?

options.text: Genie failed to learn language after being isolated during the critical period
The Dani, with 2 colour words, still learn other colour shades well
Washoe the chimpanzee learned about 160 signs during her sign language training
Patients with Wernicke's aphasia cannot understand speech but can still speak fluently

epc7.explanation: Rosch (1973) showed the Dani (2 basic colour terms) can learn extra colour distinctions just fine, undermining strict determinism. Later work (Himba colour categories, Boroditsky's time-metaphor studies) supports the weaker claim that language influences, without fully determining, perception — that is linguistic relativity. The other options are about critical periods and aphasia, not language-and-thought.

epc7.question: A patient with acquired dyslexia reads the non-word "refki" without difficulty but reads exception words like "pint" as if they rhymed with "mint". This is a description of _____.

options.text: phonological dyslexia
deep dyslexia
developmental dyslexia
surface dyslexia

epc7.explanation: Regularizing exception words points to a broken direct lexical route = surface dyslexia (the intact phonological route still handles nonwords like "refki" without trouble). Phonological dyslexia is the opposite pattern — nonwords fail, real words are fine.

epc7.question: A shopper prefers the 20€ option in a two-item menu, but switches to prefer the 35€ option once an unattractive 65€ third option is added, even though nothing about the first two options changed. This illustrates _____.

options.text: the sunk-cost fallacy
the conjunction fallacy
the decoy (distractor) effect
the gambler's fallacy

epc7.explanation: Adding an unattractive extra option changed the relative attractiveness of the original two — a decoy/distractor effect. The sunk-cost fallacy is about past investment, the conjunction fallacy is about combined-probability judgements, and the gambler's fallacy is about expecting random outcomes to "balance out".

epc7.question: Kahneman's prospect theory predicts that most people, when offered a 100% chance to lose $500 OR a 50% chance to lose $1,100, will _____.

options.text: gamble on the 50% chance, because people become risk-seeking when facing losses
choose the guaranteed loss of $500, because people strongly dislike uncertain outcomes
refuse to choose at all, since both have the same expected value
choose randomly, since framing has no real effect on decisions under loss

epc7.explanation: Prospect theory: people are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses — so most gamble on the 50% option rather than accept a certain loss. This is the mirror image of the gains case, where most people take the guaranteed $500 over a 50% chance at $1,100.

epc7.question: Statement I: An algorithm is guaranteed to reach the correct solution if it is applicable. Statement II: We switch to heuristics mainly because heuristics are more accurate than algorithms.

options.text: Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect
Only statement I is correct

epc7.explanation: I is correct — that is the defining feature of an algorithm. II is wrong: we use heuristics not because they are more accurate (they aren't — they are not guaranteed to be correct) but because the problem space is too large, time or information is limited, the decision is unimportant, or a heuristic simply comes to mind.

epc8.question: In Egly's two-rectangle task the cue appears at location 1. Locations 2 (same rectangle) and 3 (other rectangle) are equally far from the cue. What is found?

options.text: Responses to 2 and 3 are equally fast, because the distance is equal
Responses to 3 are faster than to 2, because that rectangle is new
Responses to 2 are faster than to 3, since attention spreads within objects
Attention is spread equally over both rectangles regardless of where the cue appears

epc8.explanation: This is object-based attention: attention spreads through the cued object, so the same-object location (2) beats the equally distant location in the other object (3). Pure space-based attention would predict equal speeds.

epc8.question: Libet's experiment is usually taken to suggest that _____.

options.text: conscious intention comes first and causes the readiness potential
voluntary movements can occur without any measurable brain activity
the readiness potential appears only after the movement begins
brain activity precedes conscious decisions to move by 300 ms

epc8.explanation: The readiness potential rises before people report deciding — about 300 ms earlier. Hence Pinker's “spin doctor”: consciousness may interpret rather than command. (The interpretation is disputed.)

epc8.question: Which finding is best explained by late selection?

options.text: Nothing is remembered from the unattended ear afterwards
A subliminal word still influences your later behaviour
Hearing your own name in the unattended stream
High perceptual load reduces distraction by irrelevant stimuli

epc8.explanation: Late selection says everything is perceptually encoded and attention selects afterwards — so a stimulus you never consciously saw can still be processed up to meaning. Option A fits early selection; C fits Treisman's attenuation; D is Lavie's load theory.

epc8.question: A patient with right parietal damage crosses off only the targets on the right of the page and judges the middle of a line far to the right. This is _____.

options.text: Bálint's syndrome
blindsight syndrome
visual neglect
pure simultanagnosia

epc8.explanation: Classic neglect: the side opposite the lesion is ignored. Bálint's syndrome follows bilateral parietal damage and has the triad of simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and psychic paralysis of gaze.

epc8.question: Which property of consciousness does binocular rivalry illustrate best?

options.text: Intentionality
Selectivity
Unity
Transiency

epc8.explanation: The content keeps changing even though the input stays the same — that is transiency. (That only one image is seen at a time also illustrates unity.)

epc8.question: Sleepwalking _____.

options.text: occurs in slow-wave sleep and waking is harmless
occurs during REM sleep and waking is dangerous
is a form of narcolepsy with sudden attacks
is caused by a failure of REM atonia

epc8.explanation: Somnambulism happens in deep slow delta-wave sleep, not REM — and the slides state explicitly that waking a sleepwalker is not harmful. REM atonia is the muscle shut-off that prevents acting out dreams.

epc8.question:
Statement I: Hypnosis improves the accuracy of forgotten memories.
Statement II: Hypnosis increases confidence in false memories.

options.text: Only statement I is correct
Only statement II is correct
Both statements are correct
Both statements are incorrect

epc8.explanation: Exactly the opposite of a common belief: hypnosis does not make memories more accurate, but it does make people more confident in memories that may be false — which is why it is problematic in legal settings.

epc8.question: Finding a red vertical bar among blue vertical bars is immediate, but finding a red vertical bar among red horizontal and blue vertical bars requires item-by-item search. This is explained by _____.

options.text: Feature Integration Theory: conjunction search requires focused attention
perceptual load theory: high load reduces distractor processing
the cocktail party effect: hearing your own name
posthypnotic suggestion: a hypnotist's cue triggers later behaviour

epc8.explanation: Treisman: single features are registered in parallel (pop-out), but binding two features into one object needs focused attention — the “glue”. Without it you get illusory conjunctions.

epc8.question: An arrow in the centre of the screen points to the likely target location, and the effect shows up only at longer SOAs. This is _____.

options.text: an exogenous cue
an illusory conjunction
an endogenous cue
change blindness

epc8.explanation: An instruction-like, voluntary cue is endogenous, and endogenous shifts are relatively slow, so they need a longer stimulus onset asynchrony. A sudden peripheral flash would be exogenous and fast.

epc8.question: Which example fits self-consciousness rather than full consciousness?

options.text: You notice a large red book lying on the table nearby
You think it is odd that a long book is here
You read the book for an hour without noticing the time
You decide not to take the book as you'd look silly

epc8.explanation: Self-consciousness turns attention to the self as an object (how would I look?). Noticing the book is minimal consciousness; thinking about the oddness is full consciousness.

epc10.question: Which statement about the difference between an emotion and a mood is correct?

options.text: A mood is a brief reaction to a specific stimulus, while an emotion lasts hours or days without clear cause.
An emotion is a short, stimulus-linked experience with a body reaction; a mood is a diffuse, longer-lasting, less intense state.
Emotions and moods are exactly the same psychological state, and differ only in the everyday words used to describe them.
A mood produces a stronger physiological reaction than an emotion does, because it is more general and lasts much longer.

epc10.explanation: This is the exact definition from the slides. A is backwards, C ignores a real distinction the course tests, and D is simply false — emotions typically have the stronger, more immediate physiological signature.

epc10.question: Patients with a spinal-cord injury (little or no feedback from the body) tend to report weaker emotions than before their injury. This finding best supports _____.

options.text: the James-Lange theory of emotion
Cannon and Bard's theory
Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory
the facial universality hypothesis

epc10.explanation: James-Lange says the feeling is the sensed body reaction, so less bodily feedback should mean weaker emotion — exactly what spinal-cord patients show. Cannon-Bard doesn't need body feedback for feeling at all; Schachter-Singer is about labelling general arousal; the universality hypothesis is about facial expression, unrelated here.

epc10.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Cannon and Bard's objections to the James-Lange theory?

options.text: The autonomic nervous system reacts too slowly to explain how quickly some emotions appear in everyday social situations.
The same bodily reaction (e.g. a racing heart) can accompany several different emotions, so it cannot define one.
People are not very good at noticing small changes in their own heart rate, temperature, or blood pressure.
Each emotion has its own pattern of bodily change, so without a bodily reaction there can be no emotion.

epc10.explanation: A, B and C are three of Cannon & Bard's four real objections (the fourth being that non-emotional events like flu also change the ANS but aren't felt as emotions). D restates the James-Lange position itself, so it cannot be an objection against it.

epc10.question: In Dutton & Aron's (1974) bridge study, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to later contact the female researcher than men who crossed a sturdy, low bridge. The best explanation is that these men _____.

options.text: felt calmer and more confident after crossing, which made them seem charming
were the ones who crossed the sturdy bridge, not the suspension bridge
misattributed their leftover fear-based arousal to feeling attracted toward the female researcher
felt no arousal at all once they had reached the far side

epc10.explanation: This is Schachter-Singer's theory in action: leftover fear-arousal from the scary bridge got reinterpreted as attraction. B reverses the actual finding, and A and D contradict the arousal that the theory says must still be present.

epc10.question: After a monkey's temporal lobes and amygdala were removed, it lost its fear of normally frightening objects, could no longer tell good food from bad food, and became hypersexual. This pattern is known as _____.

options.text: Capgras syndrome
Klüver-Bucy syndrome
acquired prosopagnosia
overjustification effect

epc10.explanation: This is exactly Klüver & Bucy's (1937, 1939) monkey findings. Capgras and prosopagnosia are human face/recognition conditions, unrelated to temporal-lobe removal in animals; the overjustification effect is about motivation and rewards.

epc10.question: You are hiking and jump back from a curled shape on the path before you consciously know what it is. A second later you see it is only a rope. According to LeDoux, the jump was driven by the _____ pathway, and recognising the rope by the _____ pathway.

options.text: fast (thalamus → amygdala); slow (thalamus → cortex → amygdala)
slow (thalamus → cortex → amygdala); fast (thalamus → amygdala)
the fast pathway through the thalamus for both events
the slow pathway through the cortex for both events

epc10.explanation: The fast, direct thalamus→amygdala route triggers the jump before you know why ("good or bad?"). The slower thalamus→cortex→amygdala route works out the details ("what exactly is this?") and lets you realise it's just a rope.

epc10.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Ekman's six universal basic emotions?

options.text: fear
disgust/contempt
jealousy
surprise

epc10.explanation: Ekman's six are happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust/contempt. Jealousy is a real emotion but is not one of the six universally-recognised basic expressions.

epc10.question: A participant watches a disgusting film while an experimenter is in the room, and keeps a pleasant expression on her face the whole time, even though disgust is what she truly feels. This display-rule technique is called _____.

options.text: intensification
deintensification
neutralizing
masking

epc10.explanation: Masking = showing a genuinely different emotion than what you feel — pleasant instead of disgusted — exactly like the Japanese students in Ekman & Friesen (1972). Deintensification and intensification would still show some disgust, just less or more; neutralizing would show no expression at all, not a pleasant one.

epc10.question: Which of the following is NOT a real difference between a genuine (Duchenne) smile and a posed smile?

options.text: A genuine smile typically lasts for a much shorter time than a posed one.
A genuine smile involves the orbicularis oculi (eye) muscle; a posed one usually doesn't.
A genuine smile is usually more symmetric across the face than a posed one.
A genuine smile has a smoother onset and offset than a posed one does.

epc10.explanation: True emotions actually last somewhat longer than posed ones, not shorter — so A is the odd one out. B, C and D are all real, textbook differences between genuine and posed smiles.

epc10.question: Rats whose ventromedial hypothalamus was destroyed will typically _____, while rats whose lateral hypothalamus was destroyed will typically _____.

options.text: stop eating and starve; overeat until obese
keep eating normally; keep eating at normal levels
overeat until obese; stop eating and starve
become hyperactive and restless; become hypersexual and aggressive

epc10.explanation: The ventromedial hypothalamus is the "off switch" for hunger, so destroying it removes the brake (gorging/obesity). The lateral hypothalamus is the "on switch", so destroying it removes hunger altogether (starving to death even surrounded by food). D describes Klüver-Bucy syndrome, not hypothalamus damage.

epm.question: Some early philosophers believed that certain kinds of knowledge were innate or inborn, a theory known as _____.

options.text: tabula rasa
philosophical nativism
British empiricism
early structuralism

epm.explanation: Nativism = certain knowledge is inborn (Plato, Descartes, Kant). Tabula rasa ("blank slate", Locke) and empiricism are the opposite view: knowledge comes from experience. Structuralism (Wundt/Titchener) is a school that broke consciousness into its elements using introspection.→ re-read Chapter 1

epm.question: Randy has only ever met his neighbour Jens in front of his house. Before meeting him in a restaurant, Randy memorises Jens's characteristics (6 feet tall, bald, white glasses, black beard, yellow sneakers, blue cane). Randy most likely suffers from _____.

options.text: prosopagnosia
color blindness
false recognition
anterograde amnesia

epm.explanation: Prosopagnosia = face blindness: you cannot recognise people by their face, so you learn to identify them by other cues (clothes, voice, a cane). Colour blindness would not stop face recognition. False recognition is remembering something that did not happen; anterograde amnesia is being unable to form new memories — he clearly can, since he memorises the features.→ re-read Chapter 4/5

epm.question: Mental chronometry (developed by Franciscus Donders) is highly valuable in modern-day research because _____.

options.text: its basic principles can be applied to many techniques and experiments
it showed that stimulus discrimination reaction time stays constant across tasks
reaction times of different tasks must be multiplied to reveal processes
it reveals the JND (Just Noticeable Difference) of each tested stimulus pair

epm.explanation: Mental chronometry = measuring how long mental processes take by comparing reaction times between tasks (the subtraction method). Its logic still underlies modern RT research and imaging. The JND belongs to psychophysics (Weber/Fechner), not to Donders; RTs are subtracted, not multiplied.→ re-read Chapter 1/2

epm.question: According to Weber's law (Weber-Fechner's law), the quantity difference between dots on two screens should be easiest to detect when _____.

options.text: screen 1 displays 6 dots, and screen 2 displays 7 dots
screen 1 displays 9 dots, and screen 2 displays 12 dots
screen 1 displays 33 dots, and screen 2 displays 42 dots
screen 1 displays 8 dots, and screen 2 displays 10 dots

epm.explanation: Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the standard, so compare the ratios. 7/6 ≈ 1.17 · 12/9 ≈ 1.33 · 42/33 ≈ 1.27 · 10/8 = 1.25. The biggest proportional difference (B) is easiest to detect.→ re-read Chapter 4

epm.question: Hyperopia can be corrected with _____.

options.text: a concave lens (- powered)
a convex lens (+ powered)
a cylindrical lens (astigmatism correction)
ordinary reading glasses for presbyopia

epm.explanation: Hyperopia (farsightedness) = the eyeball is too short, so the image falls behind the retina; a convex (+) lens converges the light and brings it forward. A concave (−) lens corrects myopia; a cylindrical lens corrects astigmatism.→ re-read Chapter 4

epm.question: After the cochlea, the next structure in which auditory information arrives is the _____.

options.text: cochlear nucleus
auditory cortex
inferior colliculus
superior olivary complex

epm.explanation: The auditory pathway: cochlea → cochlear nucleus → superior olive → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → auditory cortex. So the cochlear nucleus comes first; the others are later stations.→ re-read Chapter 4

epm.question: When information is encoded in long-term memory (LTM) via multiple routes _____.

options.text: inhibitory processes have a negative impact on recall
this is also what researchers call long-term potentiation
abstract items are recalled better than concrete ones
encoding presumably involves multiple brain areas and pathways

epm.explanation: Encoding along several routes (visual, semantic, organisational) means several brain areas are involved, which gives more retrieval paths and better memory. Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of a synapse, not multi-route encoding; concrete items (not abstract) are easier to recall.→ re-read Chapter 5

epm.question: Group 1 first learns Spanish and then French; group 2 only learns Spanish. Group 1 performs worse on a Spanish test. This may be explained by _____.

options.text: retroactive interference
the Von Restorff-effect
proactive interference
encoding specificity principle

epm.explanation: Retroactive interference = new learning (French) works backwards and disturbs older memories (Spanish). Proactive interference is the opposite direction (old disturbs new). The Von Restorff effect is better memory for an item that stands out; encoding specificity is about matching context at encoding and retrieval.→ re-read Chapter 5

epm.question: Ronnie takes daily cold showers. Every day his body adjusts to the cold after about 1 minute. This is an example of _____.

options.text: generalization
sensitization
sensory adaptation
