associative learning

epm.explanation: Sensory adaptation = sensitivity to a constant, unchanging stimulus decreases over time — the water stops feeling as cold. Sensitization is the opposite (stronger response); generalisation and associative learning require a learned association, which is absent here.→ re-read Chapter 4/6

epm.question: Tolman's experiments with rats in mazes provided empirical support for the concept of _____.

options.text: latent learning
observational learning
mirror neurons
superstitious behavior

epm.explanation: Tolman's rats learned the maze (a cognitive map) even without reward; the learning only showed once a reward was introduced — latent learning. Observational learning is Bandura; superstitious behaviour is Skinner; mirror neurons are Rizzolatti.→ re-read Chapter 6

epm.question: The knowledge about which words exist in a language is stored _____.

options.text: via a few transformational rules
by morphological recoding of words
in the deep syntactic structure
in the so-called mental lexicon

epm.explanation: The mental lexicon is your internal dictionary: which words exist, what they mean and how they sound. Transformational rules and deep structure belong to Chomsky's syntax; morphology is about how words are built from morphemes.→ re-read Chapter 7

epm.question: When we are reading out loud _____.

options.text: our eyes run ahead of the speech
fixations typically last 20 to 40 milliseconds
we regress more often for short words
saccades typically span 15 characters or more

epm.explanation: The eye–voice span: the eyes run ahead of the voice by a few words, which is why you can read fluently. Fixations last about 200–250 ms (not 20–40); saccades cover roughly 7–9 characters; regressions happen more with difficult/long material.→ re-read Chapter 7

epm.question: Humans rely more on heuristics instead of algorithms when _____.

options.text: the problem space is relatively small
the decision is considered relatively unimportant
we have access to detailed information
we are applying so-called syllogistic reasoning

epm.explanation: Heuristics are fast mental shortcuts: we use them when the decision does not matter much (or when time/information is limited). With a small problem space or lots of detailed information you can afford a step-by-step algorithm, which guarantees the right answer.→ re-read Chapter 7

epm.question: The general attempt to explain how subjective experiences arise is referred to as _____.

options.text: the Cartesian unconsciousness problem
the illusion of conscious control
the problem of anthropomorphism
the hard problem of consciousness

epm.explanation: The hard problem (Chalmers) asks why physical brain processes are accompanied by subjective experience (qualia) at all. The "easy" problems are about mechanisms. The illusion of conscious control refers to experiments like Libet's; anthropomorphism is attributing human traits to animals or objects.→ re-read Chapter 8

epm.question: Four possible target locations (1–4) are arranged in two grey rectangles; location 1 is cued. Assume the distance between 1 and 2 equals the distance between 1 and 3. Which statement is correct?

options.text: attention spreads equally over both grey rectangles, regardless of the cue location
reaction time for location 2 will be faster than for location 1
reaction time for location 3 will be slower than for location 2
attention is distributed equally across all 4 possible locations of the cue

epm.explanation: This is object-based attention (Egly, Driver & Rafal). Attention spreads within the cued object: location 2 is in the same rectangle as the cue, location 3 is in the other rectangle at the same distance — so responses to 3 are slower than to 2. The cued location itself (1) is always fastest, and attention is not spread equally over everything.→ re-read Chapter 8

epm.question: With the marshmallow test and ice-cream test, researchers typically study _____.

options.text: the development of self-awareness
chemical signaling of nutritional deficits
the capacity for self-discipline
diet-induced changes in metabolism

epm.explanation: Both are classic tests of self-discipline / delayed gratification: can you resist a small reward now for a bigger one later? They are about self-control and motivation, not about metabolism or nutrient signalling.→ re-read Chapter 10

exam.question: A researcher times reactions on a simple task and on a task that adds exactly one extra processing step, then subtracts the simple time from the complex time to find that step's duration. This method is called

options.text: mental chronometry, as used by Donders
additive factor logic, used by Sternberg
analytical introspection, used by Wundt
an operational definition used by Watson

exam.explanation: Subtracting reaction times of tasks differing by one step is Donders' mental chronometry. Additive factor logic is a related but different idea: it asks whether two independent steps simply add their times or instead interact.

exam.question: A lab runs twenty separate statistical tests on one data set and highlights the single test that came out significant. The main danger here is

options.text: a Type II error, a real effect being missed completely
low external validity because the sample is too small
a demand characteristic shaping how participants respond to the experimenter
a Type I error, a false effect appearing by chance

exam.explanation: Running many tests on the same data sharply raises the chance that something looks significant purely by chance, a Type I error. A Type II error is the opposite problem, failing to detect a real effect.

exam.question: A hospital needs to know whether a mass in someone's brain is a tumour affecting soft tissue, not just where a bone is fractured. Which scan is better suited, and why?

options.text: EEG, because its electrodes are well suited to soft tissue
PET, because its injected radioactive tracers only reach bone tissue
MRI, because its magnet is well suited to imaging soft tissue
CT, because its X-rays are well suited to imaging soft tissue

exam.explanation: MRI uses a strong magnet and excels at showing soft tissue such as tumours, while CT combines X-rays and is best for bone injuries and fractures. EEG measures electrical brain activity, not anatomical structure at all.

exam.question: A massage therapist presses firmly on a sore muscle, and the client reports the ache feeling less intense while the pressure is applied. Gate-control theory explains this through

options.text: endorphins released in the periaqueductal grey in response to the firm massage
A-beta touch fibers closing the spinal gate before pain reaches the brain
A-delta fibers closing the spinal gate instead of carrying sharp pain signals
C fibers being silenced directly by firm pressure on the sore muscle

exam.explanation: Pressure activates A-beta touch fibers, which can close the spinal dorsal-horn gate and reduce pain reaching the brain; A-delta and C fibers normally carry pain and open the gate, and the endorphin and PAG route is a separate, stress-triggered pathway.

exam.question: A shopping list contains nine different fruits and one hammer. Later, when trying to recall the list from memory, which item is a shopper most likely to remember?

options.text: Every fruit, because all related items form one single memorable category
The hammer, because it stands out as distinctive among the fruits
The first fruit, because of a strong and reliable primacy effect
The last fruit, because of a strong and reliable recency effect

exam.explanation: An item that stands out from its surroundings is remembered better than the rest, the Von Restorff effect, so the odd hammer should be recalled best. Primacy and recency describe list-position effects, not why a single distinctive item embedded among similar ones is easier to recall.

exam.question: A child who loves drawing for fun starts getting paid by a parent every time she draws. After the payments stop, she draws far less than she used to, even less than children who were never paid at all. This illustrates ___.

options.text: the overjustification effect, where external reward undermines her motivation
negative punishment, because a pleasant stimulus was taken away
extinction, because the previously reinforced response gradually disappeared altogether
the law of effect, because unsatisfying outcomes weakened behavior

exam.explanation: An external reward that later stops can undermine the original enjoyment of an activity, the overjustification effect, leaving behavior even lower than before any reward existed. This is not negative punishment, since nothing unpleasant was ever removed to discourage her drawing.

exam.question: According to prototype theory, how do people decide whether a new animal counts as a 'bird'?

options.text: by comparing it to every individual bird they can remember seeing
by checking whether it meets a fixed list of required features
by checking which features it shares with at least one other bird
by comparing it to the single most typical bird they know

exam.explanation: Prototype theory holds that categorization is organized around comparison with the single most typical category member. Exemplar theory is the main distractor, but it instead compares a new case against every stored example of the category rather than one typical case.

exam.question: A driver using a demanding navigation app on an unfamiliar, busy road fails to notice a clearly visible roadside sign, but notices the same sign easily when driving that road with the app turned off. Perceptual load theory explains this by saying that...

options.text: attention always shifts automatically toward any salient object that enters view
unattended information is weakened slightly but still reaches full conscious awareness
high task demands exhaust attention, so the sign is filtered before processing
low task demands trigger filtering, so the sign is blocked before processing

exam.explanation: Perceptual load theory (Lavie) holds that a high perceptual load uses up attentional capacity, producing early selection that filters out irrelevant information like the sign before it is processed. The main distractor reverses the theory's logic: it is high load, not low load, that produces this early filtering, since low load instead allows late selection and more processing of irrelevant information.

exam.question: According to LeDoux, which sequence correctly describes the fast emotional pathway that lets the amygdala trigger a fear response before a person consciously knows what they saw?

options.text: The amygdala sends the signal to the thalamus, which then alerts the cortex of the danger
The cortex sends the signal to the thalamus, which then alerts the amygdala of the danger
The thalamus sends the signal straight to the amygdala, bypassing detailed processing in the cortex
The thalamus sends the signal to the cortex first, which then informs the amygdala in detail

exam.explanation: LeDoux's fast pathway runs directly from the thalamus to the amygdala, so a fear response can begin before the stimulus is fully identified. The slow pathway (thalamus to cortex to amygdala) is the main distractor because it uses the same structures but adds a cortical detour for detailed appraisal, which takes longer.

exam.question: According to Descartes' dualism, the separate mind and body are said to interact through which structure?

options.text: the frontal lobe itself
the small pineal gland
the long corpus callosum
the nearby hypothalamus

exam.explanation: Descartes proposed that mind and body, though separate, interact via the pineal gland. The corpus callosum is a real brain structure but it connects the two hemispheres, which is unrelated to Descartes' idea.

exam.question: A memory experiment is carried out carefully on psychology students from a single Dutch university, with excellent internal validity. The results may still fail to

options.text: generalise well to people outside that narrow sample
show any reliable effect inside this specific study
count as a properly falsifiable research hypothesis
be analysed later with an appropriate statistical test

exam.explanation: A narrow, WEIRD sample threatens external validity, how well findings generalise beyond the study. Internal validity, whether the causal claim holds inside the study itself, is already described as excellent here.

exam.question: A patient speaks fluently with normal grammar but the sentences make almost no sense, and she also fails to follow simple spoken instructions. This pattern points to damage near

options.text: the left frontal lobe, close to Broca's area
the occipital lobe, at the back of cortex
the corpus callosum, joining the two brain hemispheres
the upper left temporal lobe, in Wernicke's area

exam.explanation: Fluent but meaningless speech plus poor comprehension is the classic pattern after damage near Wernicke's area in the upper left temporal lobe. Broca's area damage gives the opposite pattern: effortful speech with comprehension intact.

exam.question: A patient has damage exactly at the optic chiasm, where crossing nasal fibers meet uncrossed temporal fibers. What vision loss results?

options.text: total blindness in just one eye, with the other eye fully unaffected
loss of the same-side visual field together in both of the eyes
no noticeable loss at all, because only the crossed fibers were damaged
loss of the outer, peripheral part of the visual field in both eyes

exam.explanation: Chiasm damage removes the crossing nasal fibers from both eyes, which carry peripheral vision, producing outer-field loss in both eyes; one-eye blindness instead follows optic-nerve damage, and same-side field loss in both eyes follows damage beyond the chiasm, toward V1.

exam.question: A teacher wants students to remember a long list of grouped vocabulary words as well as possible on a later test. Based on classic memory research, which approach should help recall the most?

options.text: Test recognition memory instead of recall for every single word
Ask students to just reread the word list several times
Give the category name for each word group as a cue
Have students recall the words freely with no prompts given

exam.explanation: Tulving and Pearlstone found that giving the category name as a retrieval cue sharply increases how many words are recalled compared to cue-free recall. Simply rereading the list strengthens encoding but does not supply the retrieval cue shown to boost recall of grouped items.

exam.question: A hungry cat placed in a box with a lever learns through trial and error that pressing it opens a door to food, and begins pressing the lever more and more often. Thorndike explained this increase using ___.

options.text: shaping, since closer approximations of lever pressing were reinforced
the law of effect, since satisfying responses get repeated more
operant behavior, since actions that affect the environment change
latent learning, since a mental map formed without any reward

exam.explanation: Thorndike's law of effect states that responses followed by a satisfying outcome become more likely to be repeated, exactly what happened as the cat kept pressing the lever. Operant behavior is Skinner's later, broader term for behavior acting on the environment, not Thorndike's explanation for this specific result.

exam.question: After a stroke, a patient reads the written word 'chair' aloud as 'table', cannot read made-up letter strings at all, and often fails on short function words, though many content words are read correctly. This pattern best fits...

options.text: deep dyslexia (meaning-based errors)
surface dyslexia (word-regularizing)
phonological dyslexia (nonword errors)
developmental dyslexia (from birth)

exam.explanation: Deep dyslexia involves damage to the phonological route plus reliance on meaning, producing substitutions like reading 'chair' as 'table' and failure with both nonwords and function words. Surface dyslexia is the main distractor, but that pattern only regularizes exception words while nonword reading stays intact.

exam.question: A researcher asks people to pick which of two unfamiliar faces they find more attractive, then secretly swaps the photos before asking them to explain their choice. Most people miss the swap and confidently justify a choice they never made. This demonstrates...

options.text: the choice-blindness effect
Pinker's own spin-doctor idea
the blindsight guessing idea
the inner-homunculus problem

exam.explanation: This is choice blindness: people fail to notice the swap and still justify a choice they did not actually make, suggesting consciousness interprets decisions after the fact. Blindsight is the main distractor, but that involves responding to stimuli in a visually blind field after brain damage, not misremembering one's own preference.

exam.question: After drinking three cups of coffee, Mia feels her heart racing as she walks into a tense job interview and assumes her racing heart means she must be extremely nervous about the interview itself. This best illustrates which process?

options.text: Directly sensing a unique bodily reaction that itself is the emotion, as James and Lange proposed
Feeling a bodily reaction and an emotion simultaneously via the thalamus, as Cannon and Bard argued
Producing a tense facial expression that causes the matching nervous feeling to arise within the body
Interpreting general bodily arousal by using cues from the current situation, as Schachter and Singer proposed

exam.explanation: Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory says an emotion comes from general physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from the situation, which is exactly what happens when Mia relabels caffeine-driven arousal as interview nerves. James-Lange is the main distractor because it also involves bodily arousal, but it claims the sensed reaction itself is the emotion, with no situational interpretation needed.

exam.question: Listeners hear two alternating tones, one high and one low, each sounding completely on its own, yet they perceive either one galloping rhythm or two separate streams. This mainly shows that

options.text: behaviour must always be defined in measurable terms only
mental abilities evolved mainly because they aided survival
perception is a construction built on top of sensation
consciousness is nothing more than raw sensation itself

exam.explanation: This auditory streaming effect works like the phi phenomenon: separate sensations are perceived as something new, showing perception is a construction. Saying consciousness equals sensation is the structuralist claim this finding argues against.

exam.question: A theory has survived hundreds of supporting observations without a single exception appearing. According to Popper, what does this show about the theory?

options.text: it has now become a confirmed causal relationship
it has simply not yet been shown false
it has now been proven true beyond doubt
it no longer needs a clearly falsifiable hypothesis

exam.explanation: Popper argued theories can only be falsified, never proven true, since an unencountered exception may always appear later. Claiming it is now proven true beyond doubt is exactly the inductive mistake Popper and Hume warned against.

exam.question: Which brain method gives excellent temporal precision, telling you almost exactly when something happened, but relatively poor spatial precision?

options.text: MEG, detecting tiny magnetic field changes
EEG, reading electrical voltage at the scalp
fMRI, tracking changes in regional blood flow
PET, following injected radioactive tracers through blood

exam.explanation: EEG has high temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution, since scalp activity need not come from the cortex directly beneath it. fMRI and PET are the reverse: good localisation but slow, because both depend on blood flow.

exam.question: A radiologist, anxious about missing tumors, starts flagging almost every borderline scan as abnormal. According to signal detection theory, this shift mainly changes the radiologist's

options.text: response criterion, shifting it toward liberal without necessarily changing true sensitivity
sensitivity, meaning d-prime, while the response criterion itself stays completely fixed
absolute threshold for detecting any visual stimulus at all on the scan
Weber fraction used for judging size differences between tumors on the scan

exam.explanation: Flagging more scans as abnormal is a shift toward a more liberal criterion, raising both hits and false alarms without necessarily changing sensitivity (d-prime); the other options confuse criterion with sensitivity or bring in unrelated psychophysics concepts.

exam.question: Amnesic patients and healthy controls rated a list of words for how much they liked them, then took both a free-recall test and a word-stem completion test. What did researchers find?

options.text: Patients performed worse than controls on both memory tasks
Patients performed the same as controls on both memory tasks
Patients recalled words freely but failed the stem completion task
Patients recalled fewer words freely but completed stems normally

exam.explanation: Graf and colleagues found amnesic patients recalled fewer words in free recall yet completed word stems as well as controls, showing intact implicit priming alongside impaired explicit memory. Failing both tasks would mean no implicit memory was spared at all, which is not what was observed.

exam.question: A sales rep earns a bonus after an unpredictable number of calls, averaging one bonus every twenty calls. A coworker instead earns a bonus after exactly twenty calls every time. Compared to the coworker, the rep's call rate should be ___.

options.text: identical, since both schedules average out to twenty calls each
driven by elapsed time rather than the number of calls
higher and steadier, with no pause right after each bonus
lower overall, since no exact number of calls is required

exam.explanation: An unpredictable (variable ratio) schedule produces a high, steady response rate with no post-reinforcement pause and the greatest resistance to extinction, unlike a fixed ratio schedule, which causes a pause right after each reward. Both schedules are based on number of responses, not elapsed time, which rules out the time-based option.

exam.question: An infant is trained to turn its head toward a loudspeaker whenever a speech sound changes, earning a reward only after three correct turns in a row, with the reward delayed slightly after each turn. This method is called ______.

options.text: infant categorical perception
infant dichotic listening test
an infant head-turn procedure
infant high-amplitude sucking

exam.explanation: This describes the head-turn procedure, used with infants around 6 to 10 months, where the reward is delayed to confirm the turn was caused by the sound change itself. The high-amplitude sucking method is the main distractor, but it is a different technique used with much younger infants and relies on sucking rate, not head movements.

exam.question: In a split-brain patient whose corpus callosum has been cut, a word flashed only to the left visual field cannot be named aloud, even though the left hand can still pick out the matching object. What best explains this?

options.text: the corpus callosum is required for basic visual perception to occur
the right hemisphere processes the word but cannot access speech production areas
the left hemisphere receives no visual input from either visual field
both hemispheres completely lose the ability to process any written word forms

exam.explanation: The right hemisphere processes the word but, since speech production is localized in the left hemisphere, it cannot verbalize what it saw, though it can still guide the hand. The option claiming the left hemisphere gets no visual input at all is wrong because the deficit is about naming, not about general visual input to that hemisphere.

exam.question: Before a very important final exam, Noah feels extremely panicked and performs worse than classmates who feel only moderately nervous beforehand. This pattern best fits which idea?

options.text: The Yerkes-Dodson law, since performance is best at moderate arousal and drops when arousal is too high
The overjustification effect, since external pressure has replaced Noah's original intrinsic motivation to study for the exam
The facial feedback hypothesis, since Noah's tense facial muscles are causing his feeling of panic right now
The hedonistic principle, since Noah is simply trying to avoid the pain of a disappointing low grade

exam.explanation: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance, so extreme panic (too much arousal) produces worse performance than moderate nervousness, exactly as happens to Noah. The overjustification effect is the main distractor because it also concerns motivation, but it is about rewards replacing intrinsic interest, not about arousal and performance.

exam.question: A tone has a very high pitch. Why can firing-rate (frequency, or temporal) theory alone not explain how auditory neurons code this pitch?

options.text: auditory neurons completely stop firing for any tone above 1,000 Hz
the basilar membrane physically cannot vibrate at high frequencies at all
high-pitched tones never actually reach the cochlea from the middle ear
a single neuron cannot fire faster than about 1,000 times per second

exam.explanation: Neurons have a firing-rate ceiling of roughly 1,000 Hz, far below many audible pitches, so place theory, where different regions of the basilar membrane respond to different frequencies, is needed; the membrane does vibrate at high frequencies, just at its stiff base.

exam.question: In a listening experiment, people recall the last few words of a spoken list well (a recency effect). But when a spoken word immediately follows the list, this recency effect almost disappears, while a nonspeech buzzer has little effect. What does this best indicate?

options.text: Echoic memory decays within milliseconds, just as iconic memory also does
The recency effect reflects long-term storage rather than sensory hearing itself
A loud sound of any kind always disrupts short-term memory recall
A later spoken sound overwrites the fading echoic trace of the list

exam.explanation: Because a nonspeech buzzer leaves the recency effect intact but a spoken suffix wipes it out, the echoic trace for speech must be overwritten by new speech sounds (Crowder, 1972). This is a brief sensory-memory effect, not a long-term storage effect, which rules out the long-term-storage option.

exam.question: A toddler watches her older brother get scolded for touching a hot stove, and afterward avoids touching it herself, even though nothing ever happened to her directly. This is best explained by ___.

options.text: classical conditioning, since the stove became paired with her pain
habituation, since repeated exposure reduced her interest in the stove
observational learning, since she learned the consequence by watching
operant conditioning, since her own behavior was directly punished

exam.explanation: The toddler learned the stove's consequence purely by watching her brother's experience, without her own behavior ever being reinforced or punished, which defines observational learning. Operant conditioning requires her own actions to be directly followed by a consequence, which never happened here.

exam.question: In the wug test, children who have never heard the made-up word 'wug' before correctly say 'wugs' when shown two of the creatures. This finding best supports the idea that plural formation is...

options.text: produced by imitating the exact plural forms heard from parents
generated by a general rule, not memorized for each word separately
learned only through direct reward and explicit correction from caregivers
possible only once a fixed biological critical period has begun

exam.explanation: The wug test shows children apply the regular plural rule to a word they have never heard, so plurals are generated by rule rather than memorized one by one. The behaviorist option is wrong because the child was never rewarded or corrected for this specific invented word.

exam.question: Participants must name the ink color of a word rather than read the word itself. When the word 'RED' appears in blue ink, they respond more slowly and make more errors than when ink and word match. This illustrates which property of consciousness?

options.text: the property of selectivity
the property of transiency
the property of unity itself
the property of intentionality

exam.explanation: Attending to the ink color comes at the expense of ignoring the automatically read word, which is selectivity. Transiency is the main distractor, but that property refers to the constantly changing content of consciousness, not competition between two sources of information.

exam.question: In a classic experiment, rats could press a lever to deliver electrical stimulation to one specific brain area, and they kept pressing it for hours, ignoring the food available in the cage. Which structure was being stimulated?

options.text: The nucleus accumbens, a limbic structure that is central to reward and reinforcement
The amygdala, a limbic structure that quickly appraises whether stimuli are good or bad
The lateral hypothalamus, the hypothalamic area that mainly switches the hunger signal on
The hippocampus, a limbic structure that is mainly responsible for forming new memories

exam.explanation: This is Olds and Milner's self-stimulation study, which showed that the nucleus accumbens drives reward and reinforcement so strongly that rats pressed the lever instead of eating. The amygdala is the tempting distractor because it is also a limbic structure, but its job is appraising whether a stimulus is good or bad, not generating pleasure.

exam.question: After spinning rapidly on a playground roundabout, a child stops and suddenly feels nauseous and dizzy while standing still. This reaction mainly reflects a mismatch between

options.text: what the semicircular canals report and what the otoliths report back
what the proprioceptive system reports and the auditory system reports
what the olfactory system reports and the gustatory system reports too
what the vestibular system reports and what the visual system reports

exam.explanation: Motion sickness arises when visual input, the world looks still, conflicts with vestibular input, the canals still signal rotation, confusing the brain; canals-versus-otoliths and smell-versus-taste mismatches are not the mechanism behind motion sickness.

exam.question: People rated a list of words for how useful each would be if stranded in the wilderness, for planning a house move, or for how pleasant each word sounded, then took a surprise memory test. Which group recalled the most words?

options.text: The group that rated words for a house-move scenario
All three groups ended up recalling about the same amount
The group that rated words for their survival relevance
The group that rated words for how pleasant they sounded

exam.explanation: Rating words for survival relevance produces unusually deep, elaborate processing, which leads to the best recall of the three conditions. Pleasantness judgments are comparatively shallow processing, so that group remembers fewer words, not more.

exam.question: Honeybees were rewarded with sugar only for choosing paintings by one artist over another, with color and brightness matched. Later, bees chose a brand-new, never-seen painting by the rewarded artist. What does this best show?

options.text: The bees learned the task by observing other trained honeybees
The bees generalized the learned rule to new, similar paintings
The bees could discriminate between any two individual paintings
The bees became sensitized to visual stimuli over repeated trials

exam.explanation: Because the bees responded correctly to a completely new painting by the rewarded artist, they generalized the learned rule to similar stimuli rather than memorizing specific images. Discrimination would instead mean telling two particular paintings apart, not transferring a rule to unseen ones.

exam.question: Jim, a hearing child of deaf parents, had poor language skills at age three even though he watched television and listened to the radio daily, but he improved quickly once people began speaking directly to him. This best supports ______.

options.text: the critical-period account of language growth
the interactionist account of language growth
the nativist explanation of language growth
the behaviorist explanation of language growth

exam.explanation: Jim's language only improved once meaningful social interaction began, which supports the interactionist view that biology alone is not enough. The nativist explanation is the main distractor, but it predicts language would emerge from an innate device given input, which does not fit why Jim needed direct interaction specifically.

exam.question: Which theory explains dreaming as the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity generated during sleep, rather than as a disguised expression of unconscious wishes?

options.text: the activation-synthesis theory
Freud's wish-fulfillment theory
the information-processing theory
the memory-consolidation theory

exam.explanation: Activation-synthesis theory says dreams are the brain's attempt to make a coherent story out of random neural activation during sleep. Freud's theory is the main distractor, since it instead claims dreams are a symbolized expression of repressed wishes.

exam.question: Which chemical messenger is released by fat cells and signals the hypothalamus to reduce hunger?

options.text: Ghrelin, a hormone released by the stomach that raises the feeling of hunger overall
Testosterone, the hormone that mainly drives the sex drive in males and females
Adrenalin, a hormone from the adrenal glands that stimulates sympathetic arousal throughout the body
Leptin, a hormone released by fat cells that lowers the feeling of hunger overall

exam.explanation: Leptin is released by fat cells and sends an anorexigenic signal to the hypothalamus, reducing hunger. Ghrelin is the tempting distractor because it is also a hunger-related hormone, but it is produced by the stomach and increases hunger rather than reducing it.

exam.question: After staring at a bright red logo for about 30 seconds and then looking at a plain white wall, a person briefly sees a greenish afterimage. This best illustrates

options.text: rod adaptation, since rods are said to cause all afterimage experiences
a temporary failure of the brain to fill the blind spot
opponent-process coding, where a fatigued red-green ganglion channel rebounds toward green
trichromatic coding, where fatigued cone receptors simply stop responding to red

exam.explanation: Afterimages arise at the opponent-process, ganglion-cell level, where a red-green channel fatigued by red rebounds toward green; trichromatic theory describes receptor-level wavelength coding and does not by itself predict the colour reversal, and rods contribute nothing to colour.

exam.question: People classified novel dot patterns equally accurately whether told to search for structure or given no instructions at all, yet brain scans showed different activity patterns between the two groups. What does this indicate?

options.text: Only explicit learning can ever produce correct classification of patterns
Brain activity is always identical whenever behavioral accuracy is matched
Explicit and implicit learning reach equal accuracy via different brain paths
Implicit learning always produces better accuracy than explicit learning does

exam.explanation: Reber and colleagues found explicit and implicit learners reached similar accuracy but relied on different brain regions, showing one behavioral outcome can arise from different underlying processes. Equal accuracy clearly did not mean equal brain activity, which rules out the option claiming identical activity.

exam.question: To hang a picture, a man needs something heavy to pound in a nail. A heavy glass paperweight sits right on his desk, but he drives to a store to buy a hammer instead of using it. This best illustrates...

options.text: analogical reasoning
functional fixedness
a means-end analysis
a sunk-cost fallacy

exam.explanation: Seeing the paperweight only in terms of its usual function and failing to see it as a potential hammer is functional fixedness. Means-end analysis is the main distractor, but that term refers to breaking a goal into sub-goals, not to being blocked by an object's fixed function.

exam.question: During a ventriloquist show, the performer's voice seems to come from the moving puppet's mouth rather than from the performer. This happens because

options.text: the synchronized visual event pulls the perceived location of the sound toward it
the sound and the visual event fuse together into one new blended sound
the puppet's moving mouth is relocated toward the true source of the sound
the superior colliculus actively suppresses the sound signal until the show is over

exam.explanation: In the ventriloquist effect, a synchronized visual event shifts where a sound seems to come from; this differs from the McGurk effect, where mismatched sound and lip-shape fuse into a new perceived sound rather than just a relocated one.

exam.question: Which statement about ape language research is correct?

options.text: Washoe the bonobo used a symbol board and produced about eight hundred novel word combinations
Kanzi the chimpanzee learned about one hundred sixty hand signs and combined them into new phrases
Washoe the chimpanzee used a symbol board and correctly followed most spoken requests at age nine
Kanzi the bonobo used a symbol board and, by age nine, handled most spoken requests

exam.explanation: Kanzi was a bonobo who used a symbol board and, by age nine, correctly carried out about 72 percent of hundreds of spoken requests. The main distractor swaps the facts onto Washoe, who was actually the chimpanzee that learned roughly 160 hand signs rather than using a symbol board.

exam.question: For a given observer, the Weber fraction for lifting weights is 4%. Using a standard weight of 250 g, about how heavy must a comparison weight be for the difference to be noticed on half the trials?

options.text: about 254 g, since the JND is a fixed 4 g regardless of the standard
about 300 g, since the JND is always a large fixed share of any standard
about 250 g, since changes smaller than 10% can never be detected at all
about 260 g, since the JND equals 4% of the 250 g standard weight

exam.explanation: Weber's law states the JND is a constant proportion of the standard, so 4% of 250 g is 10 g, giving 260 g; the other options wrongly treat the JND as a fixed gram amount or invoke an unrelated fixed rule.

exam.question: In the Hermann grid illusion, faint grey ghost dots appear at the crossings of white bands on a black grid. This happens because receptive fields at the crossings

options.text: belong to cones instead of rods, which cannot process black-and-white patterns
are wired through the opponent-process red-green color channel instead of brightness
receive more surround inhibition, so they fire more slowly than mid-band fields
receive no surround input at all, so they fire at maximum rate

exam.explanation: A crossing is bordered by white on more sides than a mid-band location, so its centre-surround receptive field gets extra lateral inhibition and fires more slowly, looking darker; the cone/rod and opponent-colour options are unrelated to this brightness illusion.

exam.question: Two observers have identical sensory sensitivity, but one says "yes, I noticed it" even for very faint, uncertain stimuli, while the other says "yes" only when completely sure. The first observer will appear to have a

options.text: higher d-prime score, caused by a genuinely superior sensory detection ability overall
lower detection threshold, caused by a liberal criterion, not truly greater sensitivity
higher detection threshold, caused by a conservative criterion, despite equal sensitivity
larger Weber fraction, caused by genuinely reduced sensitivity to the stimulus itself

exam.explanation: A liberal criterion makes someone say yes more readily, which lowers their apparent threshold without changing true sensitivity; the conservative-criterion option describes the opposite responder, and the Weber fraction and d-prime options wrongly treat a criterion shift as a sensitivity change.

exam.question: Two ships use a very low-pitched foghorn to signal their position in dense fog. A listener trying to localize the sound will mainly rely on

options.text: ITD, since low frequencies bend around the head and arrive equally loud
ILD, since low frequencies create a strong acoustic shadow at one ear
the cone of confusion, which only arises for low-pitched foghorn sounds
the superior colliculus, which mainly analyzes loudness differences between the two ears

exam.explanation: Low frequencies bend around the head, so loudness barely differs between the ears, leaving the arrival-time gap (ITD) as the informative cue; ILD instead works best for high frequencies, which cast a strong acoustic shadow.

exam.question: Which part of the eye contributes the largest share of the bending (refraction) of incoming light, before it reaches the lens?

options.text: the curved, transparent cornea at the very front of the eye
the flexible lens, which is adjusted by the ciliary muscles
the pupil, whose size is controlled by muscles in the iris
the light-sensitive retina, which lines the back of the eye

exam.explanation: The cornea does about 80% of the eye's total refraction because it is curved and denser than air; the lens only fine-tunes the remaining 20%, while the pupil and retina do not bend light at all.

exam.question: Which sense sends its receptor signals directly onward without first passing through a relay station in the thalamus?

options.text: vision, which projects from the retina straight onward to the visual cortex
hearing, which projects from the cochlea straight onward to the auditory cortex
touch, which projects from the skin straight onward to the somatosensory cortex
smell, which projects from the olfactory epithelium straight to the olfactory bulb

exam.explanation: Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without first passing through the thalamus; vision relays through the lateral geniculate nucleus and hearing through the medial geniculate body, both in the thalamus, before reaching their cortical areas.

cp.question: Sanne (34) is on sick leave with exhaustion. Her company doctor advised an assessment, her husband made the appointment, and her employer pays and wants a short report on her work capacity. What must the psychologist do before anything is sent to the employer?

options.text: Get Sanne's consent and send only the work-capacity conclusion
Get the employer's approval and send the complete assessment report
Follow the commissioning contract and send the full report
Ask her husband for permission and send a short summary

cp.explanation: Sanne is the client, so she decides what may be shared, and only what is needed (a conclusion about work capacity) goes out (privacy/GDPR). The employer pays but does not own the information, and a contract with the employer does not replace her consent. The husband is only the referring party, so he cannot give consent.

cp.question: In the same case (Sanne, exhausted, employer pays for the assessment), which risk for the quality of the information does this set-up create?

options.text: The report becomes too long because several parties give input
Sanne may under- or overreport because the employer has an interest
Sanne's husband may answer instead of her during the sessions
The company doctor may change the diagnosis after the assessment

cp.explanation: The employer wants a particular outcome, so the situation is partly coerced. Sanne may underreport (to return to work) or overreport (to be taken seriously). The stance is to be curious about the function of the distortion, not to moralise. The other options are not risks the lecture names.

cp.question: A client says: "Since the divorce I just sit at home. My friends call, but I don't pick up." The psychologist replies: "It sounds like you feel lonely, and maybe also a bit ashamed to talk to them." Which skill is this?

options.text: Verbal following, because it invites the client to continue
Paraphrase, because it repeats the content in different words
Reflection of feeling, because it names the underlying emotion
Open question, because it asks for a concrete situation

cp.explanation: A reflection of feeling names the emotion behind the words and goes one step deeper than a paraphrase. Verbal following is only "mm-hm", a paraphrase repeats the content, and an open question asks for something (here nothing is asked).

cp.question: The same client says: "Since the divorce I just sit at home. My friends call, but I don't pick up." The psychologist asks: "Why don't you just call them back?" What is the problem with this response?

options.text: It is a closed question, so the client says little
It is a paraphrase, so the client feels unheard
It is a nuancing remark, so the client feels corrected
It asks for justification and jumps to a solution

cp.explanation: A why-question makes the client feel he must justify himself, and it hides advice (the solution reflex). It is an open question, not a closed one, and not a paraphrase or nuancing. A better version: "Do you have an idea what makes it hard to call them back?"

cp.question: A psychologist says: "I wonder whether staying home and the sad feelings keep each other going. How do you see that?" Which skill is this, and when is it used?

options.text: Nuancing empathy, offered tentatively during the second phase
Reflection of feeling, used mainly in the first phase
Summarizing, used mainly at the end of intake sessions
Confrontation, used only once the diagnosis is certain

cp.explanation: Nuancing empathy offers a possible connection in a questioning tone so the client can correct it. It belongs to the second phase, after safety is built. Reflection of feeling stays closer to what the client said, summarizing collects what was said, and confrontation is not what this sentence does.

cp.question: Lina (9) has these WISC-V index scores: VCI 108, VSI 102, FRI 106, WMI 82, PSI 97. Which pair gives the mean index score (MIS) and the deviation of the WMI from it?

options.text: MIS 97, WMI deviates by -15
MIS 99, WMI deviates by -17
MIS 102, WMI deviates by -20
MIS 95, WMI deviates by -13

cp.explanation: MIS = (108 + 102 + 106 + 82 + 97) / 5 = 495 / 5 = 99. The WMI is 82 - 99 = -17, so it is a possible weakness. The other pairs come from wrong averages.

cp.question: Lina's WMI (82) is 17 points below her mean index score. Which three questions must be answered before you call it a real weakness?

options.text: Is it reliable, valid, and normed?
Is it verbal, nonverbal, and age-appropriate?
Is it significant, unusual, and clinically relevant?
Is it stable, severe, and easily treatable?

cp.explanation: Significant: is the difference larger than measurement error (critical value)? Unusual: how many children in the norm group show a difference this big (base rate)? Relevant: does it fit the complaints, test observations and daily life? The other lists mix test-quality or treatment concepts.

cp.question: Which report sentence about Lina's WMI of 82 follows the lecture's recommended style?

options.text: Lina has poor working memory, which probably points to ADHD.
Lina's WMI of 82 proves she cannot remember any instructions.
Lina scored lowest on the WMI, so she needs special education.
Her lower WMI (82) fits the teacher's report; test this further.

cp.explanation: A dip in a profile is at most a reason for a testable hypothesis that links to complaints and daily functioning. It never proves a deficit, a diagnosis such as ADHD, or a placement decision.

cp.question: Which method fits best for finding out at what age a 5-year-old started walking and talking?

options.text: Interview with the parents (hetero-anamnesis) today
Maximum performance test given to the child
Self-report questionnaire filled in by the child
Structured observation at the child's school today

cp.explanation: A developmental history is collected by interviewing the parents (hetero-anamnesis). A 5-year-old cannot report this, a performance test shows current skill, and school observation cannot reveal early milestones.

cp.question: A psychologist wants to know how a client's mood changes over the day in daily life. Which method fits best?

options.text: Retrospective questionnaire asking about last month's mood
Self-monitoring with a diary app several times daily
Maximum performance test repeated during each session
Structured observation by the psychologist at the office

cp.explanation: Self-monitoring (ESM or a diary app) lets the client record mood several times a day in real life, which shows frequency, severity and fluctuation. A retrospective questionnaire blurs the changes, and the other options cannot capture daily-life mood.

cp.question: Daan (10) is far behind in reading. Hypothesis: "his delay is partly explained by low general cognitive ability." The criterion set beforehand: accept if FSIQ is below 85, reject if clearly average or higher. The WISC-V gives FSIQ 104 (95% CI 98-110). What is the decision?

options.text: Accept the hypothesis, because reading is clearly delayed
Retain the hypothesis, because the interval is quite wide
Reject the hypothesis, because the interval lies above 85
Accept the hypothesis, because the score is below 110

cp.explanation: The whole interval (98-110) is in the average range and above the criterion, so low general ability is ruled out as an explanation. The reading delay does not decide the hypothesis, and the interval is not wide enough to leave it open. Continue with other hypotheses such as dyslexia.

cp.question: Which rewrite of "Emma has an IQ of 87, so she is below average and will not be able to handle a higher school level" follows the lecture?

options.text: Emma's FSIQ of 87 (CI 82-93) is below average, so a lower level fits.
Emma's FSIQ of 87 (CI 82-93) is low average; her own motivation decides everything.
Emma's FSIQ of 87 (CI 82-93) is under 100; a higher level is unrealistic.
Emma's FSIQ of 87 (CI 82-93) is an estimate; school level depends on more.

cp.explanation: Report a score with a confidence interval, compare it with the norm group, and do not jump from score to prediction. School level also depends on support, motivation and adaptive functioning. The other options predict from the score alone or misstate it.

cp.question: After four sessions a client says: "I see that I avoid calling people because I fear rejection, but I have no idea how to change that." The psychologist takes the coach role. Which checks come before the client tries something new?

options.text: Skill, confidence, a small step, and an evaluation moment
Diagnosis, DSM classification, treatment goal, and an expected prognosis
Insight, medication, motivation, and a referral to other specialists
Empathy, confidentiality, informed consent, and a written treatment contract

cp.explanation: Insight is there but action is not, so the coach checks: can he (skill), does he dare (confidence), is there a plan (a small step), and a follow-up (when to evaluate). The other lists belong to other tasks such as classification, referral or the initial contract.

cp.question: Tim (4) has always wet the bed and is otherwise fine. Eva (11) was dry for years, started wetting the bed two months ago after her parents separated, and now refuses sleepovers. Which comparison using Rutter's criteria is correct?

options.text: Tim's problem weighs heavier, because he always wet nightly
Eva's problem weighs heavier: recent, stress-related, and interfering socially
Both weigh equally, because the behaviour is the same
Eva's problem weighs lighter, because she was dry before

cp.explanation: Eva's bedwetting is not age-appropriate, has a recent onset, follows psychosocial stress and interferes with social life. Tim's is common at 4 and does not interfere. The same behaviour can have different severity depending on context.

cp.question: Ten minutes into an intake the client gives short answers, says "I don't know" often, sounds defensive and has corrected your summary twice. What is the best response?

options.text: Ask more questions faster and explain the purpose of intake again
Fill the silences with longer explanations until the client agrees
Name the process, slow down and check you are on track
Move on to the test materials to restore some structure

cp.explanation: The signals show the conversation is not flowing, and the quality of the information depends on safety. Pushing harder, explaining more or hiding behind structure makes it worse. Name what is happening, slow the pace, check the direction, and offer a choice.

pe.question: Floor has formulated a hypothesis in which she examines the coping of a client with depressive symptoms. She uses the Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations (CISS) questionnaire to identify which coping style her client uses in stressful situations. Floor wants to formulate a testing criterion to evaluate the CISS results. Which formulation of a testing criterion is most appropriate?

options.text: The score on the avoidance-oriented coping scale is 15 or higher
The client deviates from the mean on the avoidance-oriented coping scale
The client’s avoidance-oriented coping is inadequate
The score on the avoidance-oriented coping scale is higher than the client’s score on the task-oriented coping scale

pe.explanation: A testing criterion must be concrete, measurable and set in advance (Lecture 8: decide beforehand what result counts as "supported"). A fixed cut-off (15 or higher) is exactly that. B is vague (how far from the mean?), C is a judgement, not a measurable criterion, and D compares two scales without saying what supports the hypothesis.

pe.question:
Which interviewing skills does the clinician apply in the following example?
Client: “Since I became a team leader, I have been sleeping poorly.”
Clinician: “You are saying that the new role makes you feel uneasy.”
Client: “Yes, I am afraid I cannot handle it.”
Clinician: “Can you describe a recent situation in which that feeling was strong?”

options.text: Concretizing and reflecting
Asking questions and verbal following
Showing empathy and paraphrasing
Reflecting and asking open-ended questions

pe.explanation: "The new role makes you feel uneasy" names the feeling behind the words = reflecting. "Can you describe a recent situation…" asks for one concrete moment = concretizing (Lecture 3's own example: "Can you tell me about a recent moment when…"). D is the trap: the second turn is technically an open question, but the skill being used is concretizing.

pe.question: The clinician has prepared an overview of one or more recommendations for an intervention. The recommendations have been aligned with the client’s desired goal and take possible indications and contraindications into account. At what point in the diagnostic cycle does the clinician prepare this overview?

options.text: As input for the indication analysis (IA)
As an outcome of the indication analysis (IA)
As an outcome of the advisory phase
As an outcome of the integrative formulation

pe.explanation: The indication analysis weighs the options (goal, indications, contraindications, probability, utility) and its output is the recommendation(s). That overview is then presented and discussed in the advisory phase, so it is not an outcome of the advisory phase (C), and the integrative formulation (D) comes before the IA.

pe.question: At the beginning of the diagnostic cycle, clinicians may experience the “I-have-to-do- something-now” syndrome. What does this refer to?

options.text: The clinician immediately gives advice without conducting a thorough analysis of the complaint
The clinician systematically examines both the client’s problems and strengths
The clinician focuses primarily on a process in which the client develops their own insights
The clinician starts collecting as much diagnostic information as possible before clarifying the referral question

pe.explanation: The "I-have-to-do-something-now" syndrome is the solution reflex (Lecture 4): giving advice before the complaint and help-seeking question have been properly analysed. B and C describe good practice; D describes collecting without a clear question, a different mistake.

pe.question: At which stage of the diagnostic cycle do the clinician and client determine the appropriate approach or intervention?

options.text: Integrative formulation
Indication analysis
Advisory phase
Complaint analysis

pe.explanation: Official answer key: B, indication analysis. The indication analysis is the step where the appropriate approach or intervention is determined (can/should we intervene → goals → interventions → expected utility, Lecture 9). The advisory phase (C) is where that recommendation is then discussed with the client; the integrative formulation (A) explains the problems, and the complaint analysis (D) comes much earlier.

pe.question: During the feedback session when the advice is given, the diagnostic work is, among other things, checked against the client’s responses. Which conversational mode is most required at that point?

options.text: Influencing mode
Consensus mode
Information mode
Exploration mode

pe.explanation: Checking your diagnostic work against the client's responses is the step "evaluation by the diagnostician", which slide 40 of Lecture 9 pairs with the information mode. Consensus (+ influence) only comes in the next step, the consultation about the recommendation. Exploration mode is not one of the three modes.

pe.question: In which WISC-V subtest does the child first view an image for a specified amount of time and then select puzzle pieces that together form the image?

options.text: Block Design
Visual Puzzles
Matrix Reasoning
Coding

pe.explanation: Visual Puzzles (VSI): the child views a completed puzzle and picks the pieces that together make it. Block Design = rebuilding a pattern with blocks; Matrix Reasoning = completing a matrix; Coding = copying symbols with a key.

pe.question: Murat has experienced memory complaints and headaches since a reorganization at work. His supervisor requests an independent psychological assessment. In the draft report, the psychologist concludes that the complaints are mainly related to psychosocial work stress. There is no indication of a neurological cause. Murat disagrees with this conclusion. Can he prevent the report from being sent to the commissioning party?

options.text: No, he cannot block the report from being sent, but he can temporarily delay its release until possible objections have been examined
Yes, he can block the report without giving a reason
Yes, he can block the report, but this depends on the substantive objections he has
No, because the commissioning party has the right to receive the report once the assessment has been completed

pe.explanation: Lecture 9: the client has a right to block the report to an external commissioning party; the only exception is an assessment that is not voluntary under a legal measure (then the client's objections are added to the report). This is a supervisor's request, not a legal measure, and the right to block does not depend on giving reasons, so Murat can block it. A, C and D wrongly limit his right.

pe.question: During which step of the diagnostic cycle does the clinician examine the meaning of the complaints for the client?

options.text: Referral
Complaint Analysis
Problem Analysis
Explanatory Analysis

pe.explanation: The complaint analysis centres the client's own story: what the complaints mean to the client and what help they want. The problem analysis objectifies the problems; the explanatory analysis looks for causes.

pe.question: Elise (15) has had frequent conflicts with her parents in recent months and often feels tense and low. After an intense argument at home, during which she slams doors and says that “none of it matters anymore,” her parents become very concerned. They decide to call the general practitioner, but because the situation escalates, Elise is taken to the Emergency Department (ED) by her father that same evening. At the ED, Elise briefly speaks with a physician and then with the ED psychiatrist. During this conversation, Elise says that she is often angry and sad, has difficulty sleeping, and sometimes thinks she would be better off gone. The ED psychiatrist concludes that immediate admission is not necessary, but that further assessment and treatment are indicated. He therefore refers her to the outpatient child and adolescent psychiatry clinic. A few days later, the clinic’s intake team contacts Elise and her father by phone to schedule an appointment. Who is the referrer in this case?

options.text: The general practitioner
The ED psychiatrist
There is no referrer (the outpatient clinic initiates contact)
The father

pe.explanation: The referrer is the professional who, within a professional relationship, advised that assessment is needed: the ED psychiatrist. The father is the referring party only if he makes first contact (here the clinic calls); the GP was called but never referred her.

pe.question: A student can repeat digits forward but struggles with repeating them backward and with mental arithmetic. Which WISC-V index best fits this pattern?

options.text: Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI)
Visual Spatial Index (VSI)
Working Memory Index (WMI)
Fluid Reasoning Index (FRI)

pe.explanation: Digit Span backward and mental arithmetic both demand holding and manipulating information in mind = Working Memory Index (WMI). Forward repetition alone is mainly attention span; the backward and arithmetic difficulties point to WMI.

pe.question: During the psychologival assessment, Jade considers whether the mood complaints have negative consequences for her client and/or the client’s environment. She also asks herself whether the complaints occur in isolation or not. Under which phase of the diagnostic cycle do these activities fall?

options.text: Case inventory
Severity assessment
Complaint analysis
Problem analysis

pe.explanation: Negative consequences for the client/environment and "isolated or not?" are Rutter's criteria, the tools of the severity assessment (step 3 of the problem analysis). D is too broad; the question asks for the specific activity.

pe.question:
What error does the clinician make in the example below?
Client: “I think my colleagues are excluding me.”
Clinician: “So they are indeed excluding you… It makes sense that you feel this way.”

options.text: Generalizing interpretations
Reflecting feelings
Going along with the client’s interpretation
Prematurely reassuring the client

pe.explanation: The clinician confirms "they are indeed excluding you": that is going along with the client's interpretation. A neutral response would reflect the experience ("you feel excluded") without taking the interpretation over as fact.

pe.question: Which approach explicitly refers to fluid and crystallized abilities?

options.text: Spearman’s theory
Thurstone’s theory
Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory
Gardner’s theory

pe.explanation: Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) builds on Cattell and Horn's fluid (Gf) vs crystallized (Gc) distinction. Spearman = g + specific factors; Thurstone = seven primary mental abilities; Gardner = multiple intelligences.

pe.question: Lisa is 29 years old and works full-time in the IT sector. Over the past few months, she has increasingly felt burned out. She continuously worries about her performance, sleeps poorly at night, often sleeps late during the day, and experiences a recurring sense of meaninglessness. As a result, her work performance declined, which reinforces her fear of falling short. She began to cancel social commitments, which makes her feel lonely and leads to even more worrying. Lisa has already tried to introduce more structure (stricter bedtimes, planning tasks), but notices that this works in the short term while seeming to make the worrying worse in the longer term. She feels trapped in a vicious cycle. The psychologist decides to work with Lisa from the perspective of Problem-Sustaining Patterns. Which of the following statements best fits the Problem-Sustaining Patterns perspective as outlined by Voerman et al.?

options.text: Lisa displays a set of symptoms that fit a DSM disorder, with an underlying defect as their cause.
Lisa’s worrying, sleep disturbance, and socially avoidant behavior are components of a dynamic whole that undermines her attempts to resolve her complaints.
Lisa has a biological dysfunction that primarily manifests in her sleep problems, with the psychological complaints being secondary.
Lisa’s complaints are best understood as separate symptoms that should each be treated independently to prevent mutual influence.

pe.explanation: Voerman et al. see a mental problem as a problem-sustaining pattern: a dynamic whole of interacting factors (worry ↔ poor sleep ↔ avoidance) that undermines the person's own attempts to solve it. A and C assume an underlying defect/dysfunction (what they reject); D treats symptoms as separate.

pe.question: What is the aim of the HiTOP framework within psychopathology?

options.text: To describe psychopathology based on dimensional hierarchies of symptoms and traits.
To replace neurobiological domains with symptom networks.
To develop diagnostic categories that are independent of underlying dimensions.
To classify psychopathology primarily on the basis of discrete DSM categories and diagnostic thresholds.

pe.explanation: HiTOP describes psychopathology with dimensional, hierarchical structures of symptoms and traits, from specific symptoms up to spectra and the p-factor. B mixes up RDoC and networks; C and D describe category-based systems, which HiTOP was built to replace.

pe.question: During a diagnostic interview, a client becomes frustrated and says: “I don’t understand why you keep asking me all these questions. I just want you to tell me what I should do.” What would be the most appropriate response by the psychologist?

options.text: “I understand that you want an answer, so let me tell you what I think you should do.”
“Before we discuss solutions, could you tell me more about what has been bothering you?”
“I notice that you are expecting a solution from me, while I first want us to understand together what is going on. Can we discuss how we can approach this?”
“It is important that you understand that psychological assessment always requires several questions before advice can be given.”

pe.explanation: Expectations clash, so you move briefly to the meta-level and clarify the situation (Lecture 3, regulating skills): name what you notice, explain your aim, and agree together how to continue. A is the solution reflex; B ignores his frustration; D lectures him.

pe.question: Why is it important to distinguish between the different formal roles in a psychological assessment?

options.text: Because the person who initiates the assessment is always the person who is entitled to receive the results.
Because the different parties may have different questions, interests, and rights within the assessment process.
Because only professionals can formally be involved in the referral process for psychological assessment.
Because identifying the client determines which other parties may participate in the assessment.

pe.explanation: Referrer, referring party, commissioning party, client and involved parties can each have different questions, interests and rights (e.g. who receives the report). A is wrong (the initiator is not automatically entitled to results); C is wrong (non-professionals can be the referring party); D is not why roles matter.

pe.question: During an intake interview, a client says they have been sleeping poorly and feeling overwhelmed at work. Before further exploring the problems or clarifying the client’s help- seeking question, the psychologist immediately recommends reducing working hours and starting relaxation exercises. Which pitfall does this best illustrate?

options.text: Confirmation bias
Anchoring
Premature explanation
Solution reflex

pe.explanation: Advising (reduce hours, relaxation) before the problem and help-seeking question are clear = the solution reflex. Confirmation bias and anchoring are thinking errors about hypotheses; premature explanation is treating a complaint as a cause/disorder too early.

pe.question: A psychologist prepares a technical-professional report following a psychological assessment. Which approach best fits the purpose of this type of report?

options.text: Focus primarily on the conclusions and recommendations, while limiting technical details to improve readability.
Describe the diagnostic reasoning and relevant steps of the diagnostic cycle, including the sources, instruments, psychometric information, and test results used.
Report all test scores in detail, while leaving out the diagnostic reasoning to ensure that the report remains objective.
Adapt the report primarily to the client’s level of understanding, avoiding professional terminology and psychometric information where possible.

pe.explanation: The technical-professional report is for colleagues and supervisors: every step of the diagnostic reasoning, with sources, instruments, psychometric information and results, so the reasoning can be checked. A and D describe the client report; C drops the reasoning, the most important part.

sym.question: A client with long-standing depression is referred for assessment. The professional notices signs that might point to autism. What does the symposium suggest doing first?

options.text: Ask what the client wants to work on first, and stabilise before more testing
Run the autism assessment first, so treatment can target the right diagnosis
Test for every possible condition at once, so nothing is overlooked later
Postpone all contact until the full diagnostic picture is completely clear

sym.explanation: Laura was tested for autism and giftedness before her depression was treated, and felt the depression itself was overlooked. Lesson: start with what matters most to the person, stabilise with support, and let further assessment serve the person rather than become the focus.

sym.question: Karin contrasted two questions a professional can ask. Which one did she recommend, and why?

options.text: "What is wrong with you?", because it leads quickly to the correct classification
"What happened to you?", because reactions can be normal responses to abnormal situations
"What do you want from me?", because it puts the request for help at the centre
"What does your family think?", because the context explains most of the symptoms

sym.explanation: Focusing only on what is "wrong" can make people believe something is fundamentally wrong with them. "What happened to you?" frames reactions as a healthy brain and body responding to an unhealthy situation — a normal response to an abnormal situation.

sym.question: A client keeps blaming herself for abuse she experienced. Which approach fits the lessons from the symposium?

options.text: Tell her firmly that her feelings of guilt are irrational and should be dropped
Avoid the topic until she raises it herself, so she does not feel pushed
Validate her feelings while helping her separate having control from having blame
Explain the diagnostic criteria for PTSD so she understands her own reaction

sym.explanation: Laura's point: acknowledge that the feelings are valid, and help the person distinguish control from blame — you can have feelings about something without being responsible for what happened.

sym.question: According to the experts by experience, how should a professional treat a diagnosis?

options.text: As an identity that helps the client make sense of who they really are
As a tool that can open up treatment but should never define the person
As a fixed endpoint that should not be questioned once it has been given
As a formality that matters only for insurance and can otherwise be ignored

sym.explanation: A diagnosis is a tool, not an identity: it can help understanding and access to treatment, but it should never replace the person's own story. Karin even received a diagnosis that didn't fit, just to get access to help.

sym.question: Which statement about recovery matches what both speakers said?

options.text: Recovery follows fixed phases with a predictable duration for each person
Recovery is complete once the symptoms no longer meet the criteria
Recovery is mainly the result of choosing the right treatment protocol
Recovery is rarely linear, and the time spent in each phase differs a lot

sym.explanation: Laura: the phases may be similar, but how long someone spends in each varies greatly, so don't expect a fixed timeline ("from surviving to living"). Karin: about 20 years of trial and error; treatment must be flexible, not one protocol.

sym.question: During an intake a client takes a long time to answer one particular question. What is the best reading, following the symposium?

options.text: The pause may be meaningful, so it can be worth exploring that topic further
The question was probably unclear, so move on quickly to the next one on the list
The client is likely avoiding the truth, so repeat the question more firmly
The client is tired, so the interview should be ended and rescheduled

sym.explanation: Laura asked for natural, responsive conversations instead of a rigid question list: a long pause can be meaningful, and rewording a question (e.g. "a bad sexual experience") can make it easier to open up.
